item.title: Alcohol and Type 2 Diabetes: UK Units, Hypo Risk and Tips
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Can you drink alcohol with type 2 diabetes? UK unit limits, how alcohol can cause a hypo, when to call 999 and simple tips for drinking more safely. Can you drink alcohol if you have type 2 diabetes? The NHS alcohol guidance applies to everyone, but with diabetes there’s one extra thing to plan for.
item.content:encoded:
Can you drink alcohol if you have type 2 diabetes? The NHS alcohol guidance applies to everyone, but with diabetes there’s one extra thing to plan for. The NHS lists drinking a lot of alcohol, particularly without eating, as a cause of low blood sugar, and it advises everyone to stay within 14 units a week. If you take diabetes medicines, ask your GP or diabetes nurse how alcohol fits with your treatment.

How does alcohol affect blood sugar?

The NHS says low blood sugar (a hypo) is usually when your blood glucose is below 4mmol/L. One of the causes it lists is drinking a lot of alcohol, particularly without eating.

The NHS also explains that diabetes medicines lower your blood sugar, but can sometimes make it go too low. This is common with insulin, and can also happen with some other diabetes medicines, such as gliclazide and glimepiride.

Your risk depends on your treatment, so your GP, diabetes nurse or pharmacist is the best person to ask.

How much alcohol is low risk?

The NHS advises men and women not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis. If you regularly drink that much, spread it over 3 or more days and try to have several drink-free days each week.

The NHS calls this “low risk” rather than “safe”, because there’s no safe drinking level. It defines binge drinking as more than 8 units in a single session for men, or more than 6 units for women.

How many units are in common drinks?

One unit is 10ml or 8g of pure alcohol. The NHS says that’s around the amount the average adult can process in an hour. Here are its figures for common drinks:

Drink Units
Single small shot of spirits (25ml, 40%) 1
Small glass of wine (125ml, 12%) 1.5
Bottle of lager, beer or cider (330ml, 5%) 1.7
Pint of lower-strength lager, beer or cider (3.6%) 2
Standard glass of wine (175ml, 12%) 2.1
Can of lager, beer or cider (440ml, 5.5%) 2.4
Pint of higher-strength lager, beer or cider (5.2%) 3
Large glass of wine (250ml, 12%) 3
Bottle of wine (750ml, 13.5%) 10

Single small shot of spirits (25ml, 40%): 1 units

Small glass of wine (125ml, 12%): 1.5 units

Bottle of lager, beer or cider (330ml, 5%): 1.7 units

Pint of lower-strength lager, beer or cider (3.6%): 2 units

Standard glass of wine (175ml, 12%): 2.1 units

Can of lager, beer or cider (440ml, 5.5%): 2.4 units

Pint of higher-strength lager, beer or cider (5.2%): 3 units

Large glass of wine (250ml, 12%): 3 units

Bottle of wine (750ml, 13.5%): 10 units

So 14 units is about 6 pints of average-strength beer or 10 small glasses of lower-strength wine. A couple of large glasses of wine can use up almost half of your weekly guideline.

You can work out units yourself: strength (ABV) x volume (ml) ÷ 1,000. A pint of 5.2% lager is 5.2 x 568 ÷ 1,000, which is just under 3 units.

How can you drink more safely with diabetes?

Based on the NHS advice, a few practical steps:

  1. Don’t drink on an empty stomach. The NHS hypo page says do not drink alcohol without eating. Waiting for your evening meal before you have a drink is one of the NHS Better Health tips.
  2. Choose lower-strength drinks. NHS Better Health suggests trying lighter beers under 4% ABV and other lower-strength drinks.
  3. Write off the rounds. This is another NHS Better Health tip for drinking less.
  4. Keep some days drink-free. This is part of the NHS low-risk guidance.
  5. Watch the calories. NHS Better Health says alcoholic drinks are high in calories. Our guide to reading food labels with diabetes can help you spot sugar in mixers and soft drinks.
  6. Know the signs of a hypo. The NHS lists feeling hungry, sweating, shaking, dizziness, feeling anxious or irritable, blurred vision and confusion.

If you drive and are at risk of hypos, the NHS says to check your blood sugar before each journey and every 2 hours while driving.

What should you do if you have a hypo after drinking?

The NHS says to treat a hypo with something sugary and quick-acting, such as a small glass of fruit juice or a sugary fizzy drink, then check your blood sugar after 10 to 15 minutes. Once it’s back above 4mmol/L, eat something longer-acting. Your diabetes team can tell you exactly how to treat hypos with your medicines.

Call 999 if you think someone has very low blood sugar and they’re not responding normally or they’re unconscious, and they’ve been drinking alcohol. The NHS also says to call 999 if a glucagon injection isn’t available or you don’t know how to use it, or if they haven’t recovered within 10 minutes of a glucagon injection. Don’t give an unconscious person food or drink, as they won’t be able to swallow safely.

See a GP if you have diabetes and you get hypos often, you’ve had severe hypos or you’ve had hypos at night. You can also speak to your diabetes care team.

Does alcohol affect blood pressure too?

If you’re also watching your blood pressure, NHS Better Health says that if you drink nearly every day, you might be more at risk of high blood pressure. Our guide to foods that can help lower blood pressure has more on eating well for your heart.

Where can you get help to cut down?

If you’d like support, NHS Better Health says you can call Drinkline free on 0300 123 1110. If you drink heavily and get physical withdrawal symptoms, the NHS says to get medical advice before stopping, because it can be dangerous to stop too quickly without proper help.

Bar snacks and pub meals rarely come with a label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs, sugar, salt and calories in a meal from a photo and suggest a lighter swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Natasha's Law Explained: Allergen Labelling Rules in the UK
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: What is Natasha's Law? How UK allergen labelling works for food packed on site, what the label must show, what isn't covered and how to check. Natasha’s Law is the UK allergen labelling rule for food that is made and packed on the same premises where it’s sold. Since 1 October 2021, this “prepacked for direct sale” (PPDS) food must carry a label with the name of the food and a full ingredients list, with the 14 major allergens emphasised.
item.content:encoded:
Natasha’s Law is the UK allergen labelling rule for food that is made and packed on the same premises where it’s sold. Since 1 October 2021, this “prepacked for direct sale” (PPDS) food must carry a label with the name of the food and a full ingredients list, with the 14 major allergens emphasised. It covers things like sandwiches, salad boxes and wrapped deli cheese that are packed before you order.

What is Natasha’s Law?

Natasha’s Law is the common name for a change to UK food labelling law that came into force on 1 October 2021. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the labelling requirements for PPDS food changed across the UK from that date.

Allergy UK explains that the law followed the death of teenager Natasha Ednan-Laperouse in 2016. She died from an allergic reaction caused by an ingredient in a baguette bought at a food outlet at Heathrow Airport. At the inquest, the coroner said the legislation at the time was not adequate and asked for a review.

What does “prepacked for direct sale” mean?

The FSA describes PPDS food as food that is packaged at the same place it is offered or sold to consumers, and is ready to hand over before it is ordered or selected.

Food usually counts as PPDS when it is fully or partly enclosed by packaging, can’t be changed without opening the packaging, and is ready for sale. The FSA gives examples such as a cake in cling film, sandwiches in a folded paper bag and rolls in a knotted or sealed plastic bag.

Examples of PPDS food

  • Prepacked sandwiches, wraps and salad boxes
  • Pies in packaging and soup already in pots
  • Prepacked paninis or boxes of pizza that can be reheated when you ask
  • Cheeses and meats from a supermarket deli counter that have already been wrapped (Allergy UK)

What must a PPDS label show?

The FSA says labels on PPDS food must show the name of the food and the ingredients list. Any of the 14 allergens in the ingredients must be emphasised, for example in bold, capital letters, a contrasting colour or underlined text.

Allergy UK adds that an allergen must be emphasised even if the ingredient comes under a different name. Its own example shows whey powder listed as “whey powder (from milk)” in bold.

The 14 allergens that must be emphasised are:

The 14 allergens
Celery Milk
Cereals containing gluten Molluscs
Crustaceans Mustard
Eggs Nuts
Fish Peanuts
Lupin Sesame seeds
Soya Sulphur dioxide and sulphites

Celery: Milk

Cereals containing gluten: Molluscs

Crustaceans: Mustard

Eggs: Nuts

Fish: Peanuts

Lupin: Sesame seeds

Soya: Sulphur dioxide and sulphites

Our guide to the 14 major food allergens explains where each one tends to hide.

What food isn’t covered by Natasha’s Law?

Not every food you buy in a café or shop is PPDS. The FSA explains how the main types differ:

Type of food Example What you get
PPDS A sandwich made and packed on site before you order Full label with name, ingredients and allergens emphasised
Prepacked elsewhere A sandwich made in a factory and delivered to the shop Full label with name, ingredients, allergens and other details
Non-prepacked or made to order Unpackaged cakes on display, an open salad bar, food made to order or packed when you ask No label needed, but allergen information must still be available
Distance selling Food ordered online or by phone PPDS label rules don’t apply, but allergen information must be given before you order and on delivery

PPDS (example A sandwich made and packed on site before you order): full label with name, ingredients and allergens emphasised

Prepacked elsewhere (example A sandwich made in a factory and delivered to the shop): full label with name, ingredients, allergens and other details

Non-prepacked or made to order (example Unpackaged cakes on display, an open salad bar, food made to order or packed when you ask): no label needed, but allergen information must still be available

Distance selling (example Food ordered online or by phone): pPDS label rules don’t apply, but allergen information must be given before you order and on delivery

The FSA also says hot drinks made to order are not PPDS, while pre-poured drinks would be PPDS and need a label. For loose food, such as a buffet, a business can list allergens on menus or display a sign telling you to ask staff.

If you often eat out, our guide to eating out with a food allergy covers the questions to ask.

What about “may contain” labels?

The FSA describes a precautionary allergen label as a statement a business can choose to add when there is an unavoidable risk of allergen cross-contamination. It is often written as “may contain” an allergen or “not suitable for someone with” an allergy.

Allergy UK says there is currently no law on when these statements should be used. It advises that guidance on whether you need to avoid foods with these statements should come from a healthcare professional.

How can you use Natasha’s Law when shopping?

A full ingredients list on a PPDS label gives you more to go on, but it still works best alongside a few habits:

  1. Read the label every time. Allergy UK says food labels need to be checked every time a product is bought.
  2. Check new products carefully. Always check the label on anything you haven’t bought before.
  3. Ask about loose food. For unpackaged food, ask staff about ingredients and what precautions are taken against cross-contamination.
  4. If in doubt, leave it. Allergy UK says if the label isn’t clear, or you still have doubts after speaking to staff, don’t take the risk.

For home-cooked meals and food with no label, the Dietary Insight app can flag ingredients in a photo of a dish that may contain allergens on your profile, as a starting point for your questions. It can’t see hidden ingredients or cross-contamination, so always check the full label and ask the person who made the food.

When should you call 999?

The NHS says to call 999 if you think you or someone else is having an anaphylactic reaction. Signs include lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swelling, breathing very fast or struggling to breathe, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, skin, tongue or lips turning blue, grey or pale, suddenly feeling very confused, drowsy or dizzy, or someone fainting and not waking up. A child may be limp, floppy or not responding as usual.

If you have an adrenaline auto-injector, the NHS says to use it, call 999 and say you think it’s anaphylaxis. Use a second auto-injector if symptoms haven’t improved after 5 minutes. Lie down and raise your legs, or sit up slowly if you’re struggling to breathe, and don’t stand or walk, even if you feel better.

If you’re unsure whether you have a food allergy, or what you should avoid, talk to your GP.

item.title: Sweeteners and Diabetes: Are They Safe and Which to Choose?
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Can you use sweeteners with diabetes? What UK experts say about safety, blood sugar, sugar alcohols, 'diabetic' foods and reading the label. Can you use sweeteners if you have diabetes? Yes. Diabetes UK says low-calorie sweeteners give you sweetness while reducing your sugar and calorie intake, because they contain little or no calories or carbohydrate and don’t affect blood glucose levels.
item.content:encoded:
Can you use sweeteners if you have diabetes? Yes. Diabetes UK says low-calorie sweeteners give you sweetness while reducing your sugar and calorie intake, because they contain little or no calories or carbohydrate and don’t affect blood glucose levels. Using them is a personal choice, and they work best as one part of a balanced diet rather than a fix on their own.

What are sweeteners?

The NHS describes lower or no calorie sweeteners as substances used instead of sugar to sweeten foods and drinks. You’ll find them in drinks, desserts, ready meals, cakes, chewing gum and even toothpaste.

Diabetes UK says it is more useful to split sweeteners into two groups than to worry about “natural” versus “artificial”:

Type Examples Carbs and calories?
Nutritive sweeteners Sugar (sucrose), glucose, fructose, honey, syrup Yes, they contain carbohydrate and calories
Low-calorie (non-nutritive) sweeteners Aspartame, sucralose, saccharin, acesulfame K, stevia-based sweeteners Little or none
Sugar alcohols (polyols) Sorbitol, xylitol, erythritol, maltitol, isomalt Some, but fewer calories and less effect on blood glucose than sugar

Nutritive sweeteners (examples Sugar (sucrose), glucose, fructose, honey, syrup): yes, they contain carbohydrate and calories

Low-calorie (non-nutritive) sweeteners (examples Aspartame, sucralose, saccharin, acesulfame K, stevia-based sweeteners): little or none

Sugar alcohols (polyols) (examples Sorbitol, xylitol, erythritol, maltitol, isomalt): some, but fewer calories and less effect on blood glucose than sugar

Diabetes UK points out that labels such as “natural” can be confusing. Stevia products sold as natural are still processed, and sucralose is made from sugar.

Do sweeteners affect blood sugar?

Diabetes UK says low-calorie sweeteners don’t affect blood glucose levels. A joint position statement from the British Dietetic Association (BDA), the British Nutrition Foundation and Diabetes UK says replacing free sugars, including those in sugary drinks, with low or no calorie sweeteners can be an effective way to reduce carbohydrate intake and manage blood glucose after meals.

The same statement adds that sweeteners are not a stand-alone solution. A balanced diet lower in sugars, saturated fat and salt, and high in fibre, is still what matters most. It also says water is the ideal drink.

Sugar alcohols are a little different. Diabetes UK says they contain carbohydrate and calories, but have less effect on blood glucose than sugar. Because not all of that carbohydrate is absorbed, it’s unclear how they should be counted if you adjust insulin to the carbs you eat, so speak to your healthcare team for individual advice.

Are sweeteners safe?

The NHS says all sweeteners in Great Britain go through a rigorous safety assessment before they can be used in food and drink, and all approved sweeteners are considered a safe and acceptable alternative to sugar. The law also controls how much sweetener can go into which products.

Each sweetener has an acceptable daily intake (ADI). Diabetes UK explains that ADIs are set 100 times below the smallest amount that may cause health concerns, and that it’s extremely difficult for most people to reach them. The NHS says you do not need to keep track of how much sweetener you have each day.

To put that in context, the joint position statement says an adult with no other source of aspartame could, in theory, drink about 12 cans a day of a soft drink sweetened at the maximum permitted level. It stresses this is a theoretical upper limit, not a recommended amount.

The NHS adds that Cancer Research UK has said sweeteners do not cause cancer, and that there is no evidence sweeteners stimulate appetite in humans. It describes the wider evidence on sweeteners and health as mixed and limited.

Who should avoid aspartame?

People with phenylketonuria (PKU), a rare inherited condition, should avoid aspartame. The NHS says products containing it must list aspartame or E951 in the ingredients and carry a warning that they contain a source of phenylalanine.

What about “diabetic” foods and sugar alcohols?

Diabetes UK says sugar alcohols are usually used in products marketed as “diabetic” or “suitable for diabetics”. It does not recommend these products, because they can be as high in fat and calories as standard versions.

Large amounts of sugar alcohols can also cause bloating, wind and diarrhoea. The NHS says that if added polyols make up more than 10% of a product, the label must warn that excessive consumption may produce laxative effects.

Are sweeteners suitable for children?

The joint position statement says the use of sweeteners is not allowed in any foods made for children under 36 months, and that young children should not be encouraged to have products with sweeteners. For children aged 5 and over, it says sweeteners may be an option to help cut excess sugar, depending on their needs. Water and milk are the recommended drinks for children.

How to use sweeteners sensibly

Based on the UK guidance, a few practical tips:

  1. Swap sugary drinks first. The joint statement says sugar-sweetened drinks are a major source of free sugars, and diet versions may be a useful alternative for regular drinkers. Water is still the best choice.
  2. Check the whole label. Diabetes UK says “sugar-free” products aren’t necessarily low in calories, so look at fat and calories too. Our guide to reading food labels with diabetes explains what to look for.
  3. Choose the right one for cooking. Diabetes UK says aspartame loses some sweetness at high temperatures, while sucralose and acesulfame K can be used in cooking and baking.
  4. Don’t “save” calories elsewhere. The joint statement warns against eating larger portions or less healthy foods on the assumption that sweeteners have saved calories.
  5. Reduce sweetness overall. Diabetes UK says everyone should be eating less sugar, but people with diabetes don’t need a completely sugar-free diet. See how much sugar a day is recommended in the UK.

If you’re not sure whether sweeteners suit you, or how they fit with your medication, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

Desserts and drinks in cafés and restaurants rarely come with a full label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, carbs and calories in a dish from a photo and suggest a lighter swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Is Pasta Good for Diabetics? Portions, Wholewheat and GI Tips
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Pasta can fit into a diabetes diet. UK guidance on portion sizes, wholewheat swaps, GI, cooled pasta and lighter sauces to keep blood sugar steadier. Is pasta good for diabetics? Pasta can be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. The key things are the portion size, choosing wholewheat where you can and keeping an eye on the sauce, because the total amount of carbohydrate you eat has the biggest effect on your blood sugar after a meal.
item.content:encoded:
Is pasta good for diabetics? Pasta can be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. The key things are the portion size, choosing wholewheat where you can and keeping an eye on the sauce, because the total amount of carbohydrate you eat has the biggest effect on your blood sugar after a meal.

Can you eat pasta if you have diabetes?

Yes. Diabetes UK lists pasta alongside bread, rice, potatoes and plantain as a starchy carbohydrate food. It also says not everyone with diabetes needs to restrict their carb intake.

The NHS recommends that starchy carbohydrates make up just over a third of the food you eat, and suggests including at least one starchy food with each main meal. Pasta is one of the options it names.

What matters most is how much you have and what you have it with.

How much pasta is a portion?

Diabetes UK says the total amount of carbohydrate you eat has the biggest effect on your glucose levels after eating. So portion size is the first thing to look at.

Its guide portion sizes for some common starchy foods are:

Food Diabetes UK guide portion
Boiled pasta or cooked noodles About what fits in two hands cupped together (180g)
Cooked rice About what fits in two hands cupped together (180g)
Jacket potato About the size of your fist (220g)
Bread 1 medium slice (35g)

Boiled pasta or cooked noodles: About what fits in two hands cupped together (180g)

Cooked rice: About what fits in two hands cupped together (180g)

Jacket potato: About the size of your fist (220g)

Bread: 1 medium slice (35g)

Diabetes UK says these portions are a guide based on an average healthy adult, and your dietitian can advise on the portions that are right for you. It also says not to assume the portion sizes listed on food packaging are right for you.

Pasta can be tricky to measure at first. Diabetes UK suggests using the same container each time to measure out foods like pasta and rice, or weighing your food if you want to be accurate.

Is wholewheat pasta better than white pasta?

The NHS recommends higher fibre or wholegrain varieties, such as wholewheat pasta, because they contain more fibre than white or refined starchy carbohydrates and can help you feel full for longer.

According to Diabetes UK, wholegrain foods are usually better for managing blood glucose levels because they tend to have a lower glycaemic index (GI). It also says that adults should be aiming for 30g of fibre a day, and many of us don’t get that much.

There is one catch. Diabetes UK points out that wholegrains are still carbohydrate foods, and all carbohydrates affect blood glucose levels, so it’s still worth being mindful of your portion size.

What is the GI of pasta, and does it matter?

The glycaemic index ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 by how quickly they raise blood sugar. Diabetes UK says a GI of 55 or below raises blood sugar slowly, 56 to 69 at a medium rate, and 70 or more quickly. Our low GI foods list explains this in more detail.

Diabetes UK says GI doesn’t take portion size into account, and that the amount of carbs you eat has a bigger effect on blood sugar than GI alone. It gives pasta as an example: pasta has a lower GI than watermelon, but it has more carbs, so if you eat similar amounts of both, the pasta will have more of an impact on your blood sugar.

Its advice is to watch your carbohydrate portion sizes first, then choose lower-GI options as an added bonus. One of the swaps it suggests is wholewheat pasta cooked al dente.

Does cooling pasta make a difference?

Diabetes UK explains that glucose from cooked starchy foods such as white rice, pasta and potatoes is absorbed almost as quickly as glucose from a sugary drink. When starchy foods are cooled, their structure changes and the enzymes in your gut can’t break them down as easily. This is called resistant starch.

Diabetes UK says there is a small amount of research suggesting that reheating cooled starchy foods creates more resistant starch. One swap it suggests is cooked and cooled pasta in a pasta salad instead of hot pasta with sauce.

Which pasta sauces are the better choice?

The sauce can change a pasta dish a lot. The NHS says it’s the fats you add when cooking or serving starchy foods that increase the calorie content, and gives creamy sauces on pasta as an example.

Diabetes UK says protein, fat and fibre slow down the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, and foods containing them can help you feel fuller for longer and keep blood sugar levels more stable.

A few practical ideas based on that guidance:

  1. Fill up on vegetables. Diabetes UK suggests piling your plate with vegetables, as they’re naturally low in calories and high in fibre.
  2. Add some protein. Diabetes UK says protein lowers the GI of a food, so try adding beans, lentils, chicken or fish.
  3. Go lighter on creamy sauces. Use them as an occasional choice rather than every time.
  4. Check the salt in jars. The NHS says about three-quarters of the salt we eat is already in food when we buy it, including sauces.

How can I keep my blood sugar steadier after pasta?

Diabetes UK says spreading carbs evenly throughout the day and avoiding large portions all at once can help keep sugar levels stable between meals. It also suggests eating slowly, as it takes about 20 minutes for your brain to register that you’re full.

Diabetes UK also says eating more carbohydrate than usual can cause blood glucose to go too high, and eating less than usual can cause a hypo. Talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian about how pasta fits into your meals and medication. If you’d like to learn more about using GI, Diabetes UK suggests asking your GP about a referral to a registered dietitian.

For a similar look at another staple, see our guide on whether rice is bad for diabetes.

Restaurant and takeaway pasta doesn’t come with a label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs, sugar, salt and fat in a plate from a photo and suggest a lighter swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Christmas Dinner with Diabetes: UK Tips for Enjoying the Day
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: You can enjoy Christmas dinner with diabetes. UK tips on portions, hidden sugars, pigs in blankets, puddings, drinks and planning ahead for the holidays. Can you enjoy Christmas dinner with diabetes? Yes. Diabetes UK says Christmas is a time to enjoy yourself, and a short break from your usual routine is normal.
item.content:encoded:
Can you enjoy Christmas dinner with diabetes? Yes. Diabetes UK says Christmas is a time to enjoy yourself, and a short break from your usual routine is normal. A little planning, sensible portions and an eye on the extras, such as sauces, pigs in blankets and drinks, will help you enjoy the day and get back on track afterwards.

Why does Christmas food need a little thought?

Diabetes UK points out that many traditional Christmas foods tend to be higher in saturated fat, free (added) sugars and salt than our usual diets. That doesn’t mean they’re off the menu. It just helps to know where the sugar, salt and fat tend to hide.

Diabetes UK also says one or two high readings shouldn’t affect your long-term health or diabetes management, but you shouldn’t let your blood sugar stay high for long. It suggests testing more often over Christmas if you test, so you can catch changes sooner.

How do I plan ahead for the holidays?

A few practical steps from Diabetes UK make the festive period easier:

  1. Stock up on medicines. Make sure you have all the medications you need while your GP surgery is shut, and enough ketone test strips if you test for ketones.
  2. Know where to get help. If you need urgent medical advice while your GP surgery is closed, contact NHS 111.
  3. Plan around eating out. Check the menu and nutritional information online before you go. If you’re unsure how to fit a big meal around your medication or insulin, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian before the day.
  4. Keep moving. Diabetes UK says being active can help lower your blood sugar, blood pressure and blood fats over Christmas. A brisk walk, dancing or active party games all count.

What should go on my Christmas dinner plate?

The good news is that the centrepiece is a sensible choice. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) says turkey is a lean meat, as long as you avoid basting it in too much butter.

Part of the meal What the experts suggest
Turkey A lean meat; go easy on the butter when basting (BHF)
Vegetables Fill your plate with them first, and try steaming instead of frying (Diabetes UK)
Roast potatoes and parsnips Go easy, as they add fat and calories (BHF)
Pigs in blankets, stuffing and gravy Usually high in salt (BHF); try to limit processed meat (Diabetes UK)
Cranberry and other sauces Watch for hidden sugars (Diabetes UK)
Pudding Stick to one portion and think about what it’s served with (Diabetes UK)

Turkey: A lean meat; go easy on the butter when basting (BHF)

Vegetables: Fill your plate with them first, and try steaming instead of frying (Diabetes UK)

Roast potatoes and parsnips: Go easy, as they add fat and calories (BHF)

Pigs in blankets, stuffing and gravy: Usually high in salt (BHF); try to limit processed meat (Diabetes UK)

Cranberry and other sauces: Watch for hidden sugars (Diabetes UK)

Pudding: Stick to one portion and think about what it’s served with (Diabetes UK)

Diabetes UK suggests serving yourself where you can, so you’re in control of how much starchy food, protein and fat you have. It also says to watch out for festive extras like honey on vegetables, because these add free sugars.

Where are the hidden sugars and salt?

Condiments are easy to forget. Diabetes UK highlights the hidden sugars in cranberry sauce, mint sauce and prawn cocktail sauce, so a spoonful rather than a dollop is worth considering.

Salt adds up too. The BHF says sausages wrapped in bacon, stuffing and gravy are usually high in salt, and too much salt can raise your blood pressure. Diabetes UK suggests using reduced-salt stock cubes for gravy, choosing unsalted nuts and checking the labels on snacks. Our guide to how much salt a day explains the daily limit.

Diabetes UK also suggests trying to limit processed meats such as pigs in blankets, gammon, hams, pâtés and cured meats.

How can I enjoy Christmas pudding and treats?

You don’t have to skip dessert. Diabetes UK suggests sticking to one portion and swapping double cream for natural yoghurt. Its recipe ideas include a Christmas pudding with no free sugars added and “topless” mince pies made with wholemeal pastry flour, which are lower in fat and calories.

The BHF says it’s fine to enjoy the odd mince pie or chocolate. It suggests keeping to a regular pattern of meals and snacks so you don’t get too hungry, and notes that savoury nibbles like dry-roasted nuts and crisps are high in fat and often high in salt.

For a closer look at sugar limits, see our guide on how much sugar a day.

What about Christmas drinks?

Diabetes UK says you can drink alcohol if you have diabetes, unless your diabetes team has advised you not to. The UK guideline for men and women is not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.

A few tips from Diabetes UK and the BHF:

  1. Don’t drink on an empty stomach. Diabetes UK says this increases the risk of a hypo if you use insulin or some other diabetes medications.
  2. Check your mixers. Diabetes UK says a mixer with less than 2.5g of sugar per 100ml is low in sugar, and “light” doesn’t always mean low sugar.
  3. Alternate drinks. The BHF suggests alternating alcoholic drinks with water or sugar-free drinks.
  4. Know the calories. Diabetes UK says a large glass of wine is about three units and 225 calories.

Diabetes UK warns that the risk of a hypo can last up to 24 hours after you stop drinking, and that a hypo can be mistaken for being drunk. Make sure the people you’re with know you have diabetes and how to help.

When should someone call 999?

The NHS says to call 999 if someone has very low blood sugar and is not responding normally or is unconscious, and a glucagon injection is not available, they haven’t recovered within 10 minutes of a glucagon injection, or they’ve been drinking alcohol. For urgent advice that isn’t an emergency, contact NHS 111.

If you get hypos often or have had them at night, the NHS suggests seeing your GP or speaking to your diabetes care team.

How do I get back on track after Christmas?

Diabetes UK says the festive period shouldn’t affect your long-term health or diabetes management as long as you plan for it and get back to your usual habits as soon as possible. A walk on Boxing Day is a good start.

The BHF also suggests eating a bit lighter at other meals, such as soup or a salad, if you’ve had a big meal earlier in the day.

Buffets and restaurant meals don’t come with labels. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a plate from a photo and suggest a healthier swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Hidden Salt in Bread and Cereal: How to Spot It and Swap It
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: One slice of bread can hold up to a third of your daily salt, says the BHF. How to spot hidden salt in bread and cereal and choose lower-salt swaps. Is there hidden salt in bread and cereal? Yes. Diabetes UK lists bread and breakfast cereals among the main sources of salt in our diets, and the British Heart Foundation (BHF) says one slice of thick, wholemeal bread can contain as much as 2g of salt, a third of an adult’s daily limit.
item.content:encoded:
Is there hidden salt in bread and cereal? Yes. Diabetes UK lists bread and breakfast cereals among the main sources of salt in our diets, and the British Heart Foundation (BHF) says one slice of thick, wholemeal bread can contain as much as 2g of salt, a third of an adult’s daily limit. Checking labels and choosing lower-salt options can make a real difference.

Why does hidden salt matter?

The recommended maximum for adults is 6g of salt a day, which is about one teaspoon. The BHF says too much salt can raise your blood pressure, which puts extra strain on your heart over time.

Diabetes UK says we’re still eating more than that 6g, and that the recommended amount is even less for children. Its list of the main sources of salt includes bread and breakfast cereals, which most people don’t think of as salty.

Why does salt matter if you have diabetes?

Diabetes UK says salt does not affect blood glucose levels. But it’s still important to limit it as part of managing diabetes, because too much salt can raise your blood pressure.

Diabetes UK also says people with diabetes are more likely to be affected by high blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease, stroke and kidney disease. That’s why salt is worth watching alongside sugar and carbohydrate.

How much salt is in bread?

More than most people expect. The BHF gives the example of one slice of thick, wholemeal bread containing as much as 2g of salt, which is one third of an adult’s daily limit.

This isn’t a reason to give up bread. The BHF suggests comparing labels and looking for “low sodium” or “reduced salt” on the packaging.

If you have diabetes and want to choose bread for blood sugar too, our guide to the best bread for diabetics in the UK covers granary, rye and wholegrain options.

Which breakfast cereals are high in salt?

The BHF says some cereals, even those making health claims, can contain a surprising amount of salt, which is often added to boost flavour and lengthen shelf life. Here’s the salt per serving from the BHF’s breakfast cereal ranking:

Cereal (serving) Salt per serving
Porridge oats, 40g (without milk) 0.0g
Muesli with no added sugar or salt, 45g 0.01g
Whole wheat cereals and biscuits, 45g 0.02g
Muesli with added sugar, 45g 0.13g
Bran flakes, 30g 0.2g
Sugar-frosted cornflakes, 30g 0.25g
Cornflakes, 30g 0.34g

Porridge oats, 40g (without milk): 0.0g

Muesli with no added sugar or salt, 45g: 0.01g

Whole wheat cereals and biscuits, 45g: 0.02g

Muesli with added sugar, 45g: 0.13g

Bran flakes, 30g: 0.2g

Sugar-frosted cornflakes, 30g: 0.25g

Cornflakes, 30g: 0.34g

The BHF says salt levels vary between brands, so check the nutrition label before you buy. Diabetes UK’s own cereal review found that Nestlé Shredded Wheat and Weetabix were green for salt, sugar, fat and saturated fat.

How do I spot salt on a food label?

The BHF uses these per 100g guides for salt:

Salt per 100g What it means
More than 1.5g High
0.3g or less Low

More than 1.5g: High

0.3g or less: Low

Many packs also use traffic light colours: green for low, amber for medium and red for high. Diabetes UK suggests choosing foods where the salt is green or amber, rather than red.

A few tips that help when you’re in the supermarket:

  1. Compare like with like. Diabetes UK says the salt content of foods such as breakfast cereals and sandwiches can vary, so shop around.
  2. Look for reduced-salt versions. Diabetes UK suggests looking out for reduced-salt options of your favourite foods.
  3. Check the serving size. Per-serving figures assume the stated portion, so pouring a bigger bowl means more salt.

For the full picture on daily limits and other salty foods, see our guide on how much salt a day.

What are good lower-salt swaps?

A few ideas based on the BHF’s advice:

  1. Start with a salt-free wholegrain cereal. The BHF suggests wheat biscuits, some types of muesli or porridge oats.
  2. Choose porridge. The BHF says plain oats have no added sugar or salt.
  3. Swap your usual loaf. Compare a few brands and pick the one with the lowest salt per 100g, or one labelled “reduced salt”.
  4. Go easy on salty toppings. The BHF lists smoked fish and some cheeses among foods that can be surprisingly high in salt. It also notes low-fat cheese may be saltier than standard cheddar.
  5. Skip salt at the table. The BHF includes this among its tips for cutting down.

If you have high blood pressure, diabetes or kidney problems and want personalised advice on salt, talk to your GP, practice nurse, diabetes nurse or a dietitian.

What about foods without a label?

Bread from a bakery counter or a café breakfast doesn’t always come with nutrition information. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a lower-salt swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside food labels and your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Saturated Fat and Cholesterol: Foods to Watch and UK Swaps
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Too much saturated fat can raise bad cholesterol. See the UK daily limits, which foods add the most, how to read the label and simple swaps to try. How are saturated fat and cholesterol foods linked? The NHS says eating too much saturated fat can raise “bad” LDL cholesterol in your blood, which can increase the risk of heart disease and stroke.
item.content:encoded:
How are saturated fat and cholesterol foods linked? The NHS says eating too much saturated fat can raise “bad” LDL cholesterol in your blood, which can increase the risk of heart disease and stroke. Foods high in saturated fat include fatty meat, butter, ghee, cheese, cream, pastries and coconut oil. Swapping some of them for unsaturated fats, such as olive or rapeseed oil, can help.

What does saturated fat do to cholesterol?

Cholesterol is a fatty substance in your blood. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) says eating too much saturated fat can raise blood cholesterol, in particular the “bad” kind, known as non-HDL cholesterol. A high level increases your risk of heart attack and stroke.

The NHS says there’s good evidence that replacing saturated fats with some unsaturated fats can help lower your cholesterol level. So the aim isn’t to cut out fat altogether, but to change the type of fat you eat most often.

How much saturated fat a day?

The NHS gives these daily maximums:

Who Saturated fat limit
Men No more than 30g a day
Women No more than 20g a day
Children Less than adults

Men: No more than 30g a day

Women: No more than 20g a day

Children: Less than adults

The BHF says this works out at less than 10% of your calories. It adds that people who have heart disease or are at high risk may need to eat less than this. The NHS says most people in the UK eat too much saturated fat.

Which foods are high in saturated fat?

The NHS says most saturated fat comes from animal sources, such as meat and dairy, as well as some plant foods like palm oil and coconut oil. Foods high in it include:

  1. Fatty cuts of meat, sausages, bacon and pies
  2. Cured meats like salami, chorizo and pancetta
  3. Butter, ghee, lard and suet
  4. Cheese, especially hard cheese like cheddar
  5. Cream, soured cream, crème fraîche and ice cream
  6. Biscuits, cakes and pastries, such as croissants and sausage rolls
  7. Chocolate and chocolate spreads
  8. Coconut oil, coconut milk, coconut cream and palm oil

To give a sense of scale, the BHF estimates a matchbox-size piece of cheddar (30g) has about 6g of saturated fat, a tablespoon of butter about 8g, and one sausage roll about 13g.

Which foods add the most saturated fat to UK diets?

The BHF, using national survey data, says just nine foods are responsible for most of the saturated fat we eat. The biggest sources are:

Food group Share of saturated fat
Red and processed meats 15%
Cakes, biscuits, buns and pastries 10%
Cheese 9%
Pizza, pasta and rice dishes 6%
Butter 6%
Milk 6%
Chicken, turkey and dishes made with them 6%
Chocolate 5%
Egg dishes 5%

Red and processed meats: 15%

Cakes, biscuits, buns and pastries: 10%

Cheese: 9%

Pizza, pasta and rice dishes: 6%

Butter: 6%

Milk: 6%

Chicken, turkey and dishes made with them: 6%

Chocolate: 5%

Egg dishes: 5%

This is useful because it shows where small changes add up. Swapping one or two everyday foods may make more difference than avoiding an occasional treat.

Do eggs and shellfish raise cholesterol?

Not much, for most people. The BHF says dietary cholesterol does not have a big impact on blood cholesterol for most people, and lists eggs, shellfish and lean meat as foods you can still enjoy.

How you cook them matters more. The BHF says egg dishes made with butter, cheese or cream contribute much more saturated fat than a plain boiled or poached egg. If you have familial hypercholesterolaemia, the BHF says you may need to limit dietary cholesterol, so ask your GP or dietitian.

Is coconut oil a healthy choice?

The BHF says coconut oil is often reported as healthy, but there’s no scientific evidence to support this. It’s about 86% saturated fat, more than butter. Palm oil is nearly 50% saturated fat.

The BHF suggests using coconut and palm oils sparingly, as you would butter, and choosing olive, rapeseed or sunflower oil for everyday cooking. This is worth knowing if your cooking uses coconut milk or palm oil, which the NHS also lists as high in saturated fat.

What are healthier fats to choose instead?

The NHS lists these sources of unsaturated fat:

  1. Olive oil, rapeseed oil and spreads made from them
  2. Avocados
  3. Nuts such as almonds, walnuts and peanuts
  4. Oily fish, such as salmon, mackerel, sardines and trout

The NHS recommends at least 2 portions of fish a week, with 1 being an oily fish. Our guide to foods that can help lower blood pressure has more on building heart-friendly meals.

How can I read the label for saturated fat?

The NHS uses these per 100g guides, which match the traffic-light colours on front-of-pack labels:

Saturates per 100g Rating
More than 5g High (red)
1.5g to 5g Medium (amber)
1.5g or less Low (green)

More than 5g: High (red)

1.5g to 5g: Medium (amber)

1.5g or less: Low (green)

The NHS suggests choosing products with green or amber for saturated fat. Be careful with “lower fat” claims: the NHS says these must have at least 30% less fat than a similar product, but can still be high in fat. Our guide on how to read food labels explains the rest of the label.

What simple swaps can I make?

These ideas come from the NHS and BHF:

  1. Use lower-fat mince, or brown mince and drain off the fat.
  2. Choose back bacon instead of streaky, and grill it rather than fry.
  3. Try a tomato-based pasta sauce instead of a creamy or cheesy one.
  4. Use a strong-tasting cheese, such as reduced-fat mature cheddar, so you need less.
  5. Switch to 1% or skimmed milk. The NHS says skimmed has about half the saturated fat of semi-skimmed.
  6. Take the skin off chicken, and grill, bake, poach or steam rather than fry.
  7. When eating out, choose dry or tomato-based curries like tandoori, or a shish kebab instead of a doner.

If you have high cholesterol or take medicine for it, talk to your GP, practice nurse or dietitian about the right changes for you.

Checking meals when there’s no label

Home cooking and takeaways don’t come with a traffic-light label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a healthier swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside food labels and advice from your healthcare team.

item.title: Best Bread for Diabetics UK: Lower GI Choices and Label Tips
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Diabetes UK suggests granary, pumpernickel or rye over white and wholemeal bread. How to choose bread with diabetes, read the label and watch portions. What is the best bread for diabetics in the UK? Diabetes UK suggests choosing granary, pumpernickel or rye bread instead of white and wholemeal bread, because they tend to raise blood sugar more slowly.
item.content:encoded:
What is the best bread for diabetics in the UK? Diabetes UK suggests choosing granary, pumpernickel or rye bread instead of white and wholemeal bread, because they tend to raise blood sugar more slowly. Wholegrain, seeded and multi-grain breads also add fibre. Whatever bread you choose, the amount you eat matters most.

Can you eat bread if you have diabetes?

Yes. Diabetes UK lists bread alongside rice, pasta, potatoes, yams, plantain, breakfast cereals and couscous as starchy foods. These contain carbohydrate, which affects your blood sugar, but they’re also part of a balanced diet.

Diabetes UK says the total amount of carbohydrate you eat will have the biggest effect on your glucose levels after eating. So it’s less about cutting bread out and more about choosing a better type and keeping an eye on portions.

Which breads have a lower GI?

The glycaemic index (GI) is a ranking from 0 to 100 that shows how quickly a carbohydrate food raises your blood sugar. Diabetes UK groups foods like this:

GI score What it means
55 or below Low: raises blood sugar slowly
56 to 69 Medium: raises blood sugar at a medium rate
70 or more High: raises blood sugar quickly

55 or below: Low: raises blood sugar slowly

56 to 69: Medium: raises blood sugar at a medium rate

70 or more: High: raises blood sugar quickly

Diabetes UK puts breads into these groups:

Bread Diabetes UK GI group
Rye bread Low
Chapatti Medium
White bread, bagels and some types of wholemeal bread High

Rye bread: Low

Chapatti: Medium

White bread, bagels and some types of wholemeal bread: High

Its advice is: “Instead of white and wholemeal bread, choose granary, pumpernickel or rye bread.” Diabetes UK also says some mixed grain breads that include wholegrains have a lower GI than wholemeal or white bread.

The whole grains in these breads act as a physical barrier that slows down how quickly carbohydrate is absorbed. Wholemeal flour has been ground, so it doesn’t have quite the same effect. For a wider list, see our low GI foods list.

Is wholemeal bread better than white?

For fibre and heart health, yes. Diabetes UK says choosing wholegrains instead of refined carbs, such as white bread, is better for heart health. It suggests swapping white bread for wholemeal and choosing wholemeal, seeded or multi-grain bread because these are higher in fibre than white varieties.

But wholemeal isn’t automatically low GI. Diabetes UK lists some types of wholemeal bread as high GI, which is why it points to granary, pumpernickel, rye and some mixed grain breads as lower-GI choices.

Diabetes UK says adults should aim for 30g of fibre a day, but the average adult in the UK has only around 19g. Fibre-rich bread is one easy way to close that gap. Diabetes UK recommends increasing fibre gradually and speaking to your healthcare professional before changing your diet.

How do I read a bread label?

Bread names can be confusing. Here’s what Diabetes UK says the common terms mean:

  1. Wholemeal, wholewheat and wholegrain: basically different terms for the same thing, and all are wholegrain.
  2. Brown: not as high in fibre as wholemeal.
  3. Granary: contains malted wheat flakes, and may or may not be made from wholemeal flour, so check the label.
  4. Wheat-germ: made from white flour with some wheat germ added back, so it is not wholegrain.

Diabetes UK suggests looking for the words “wholemeal”, “wholewheat” and “wholegrain” on the label.

Check the salt too

If you also have high blood pressure, salt matters. Blood Pressure UK says most of the salt we eat is hidden in foods we buy ready-made, like bread and breakfast cereals. It gives the example of two similar-looking loaves where one contains 1g of salt per slice and the other contains half that.

Blood Pressure UK says adults should eat less than 6g of salt a day. Use these per 100g guides on the label to compare loaves:

Salt per 100g Blood Pressure UK rating
0.3g or less Low
0.3g to 1.5g Medium
1.5g or more High

0.3g or less: Low

0.3g to 1.5g: Medium

1.5g or more: High

Our guide on how much salt a day has more tips.

How much bread should I eat?

There isn’t one right amount for everyone. Diabetes UK says wholegrains are still carbohydrate, so be mindful of your portion sizes. On the GI page, it also advises spreading carbohydrate evenly across the day rather than eating large portions in one go.

For a sense of a wholegrain serving, Diabetes UK gives examples including:

  1. 1 large slice (40g) of multi-grain bread
  2. 1 slice of rye bread
  3. 1 wholemeal pitta bread

If you take insulin or medicines that can cause hypos, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian before changing how much carbohydrate you eat.

What can I put with bread to help?

What you eat alongside bread matters too. Diabetes UK says protein and fat both lower the GI of a food, and protein, fat and fibre slow down the digestion and absorption of carbohydrate.

A few practical ideas:

  1. Pair bread with some protein, such as eggs or beans.
  2. Add salad or vegetables to a sandwich for extra fibre.
  3. For chapattis, Diabetes UK suggests eating wholemeal chapatti and including dhal in your meals.
  4. Try freezing your loaf. Diabetes UK lists frozen and defrosted bread as a swap for fresh bread, because cooling starchy foods creates more resistant starch.

If you’d like to understand GI and portions in more detail, Diabetes UK suggests speaking to your GP about a referral to a registered dietitian.

Checking meals when there’s no label

A sandwich from a café or a homemade flatbread doesn’t come with a nutrition label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a healthier swap. It’s an estimate, so use it alongside food labels and your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: HbA1c Levels Explained: What Your Result Means in the UK
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: HbA1c levels explained: what the test measures, the NHS ranges in mmol/mol and %, how often to have it and what can change your result. A plain UK guide. What are HbA1c levels? HbA1c is a blood test that shows your average blood glucose (sugar) level over the last 2 to 3 months. The NHS says a result below 42mmol/mol (6%) is normal, 42 to 47mmol/mol (6% to 6.5%) may mean you’re at risk of diabetes, and 48mmol/mol (6.5%) or above may mean you have diabetes.
item.content:encoded:
What are HbA1c levels? HbA1c is a blood test that shows your average blood glucose (sugar) level over the last 2 to 3 months. The NHS says a result below 42mmol/mol (6%) is normal, 42 to 47mmol/mol (6% to 6.5%) may mean you’re at risk of diabetes, and 48mmol/mol (6.5%) or above may mean you have diabetes.

What does HbA1c actually measure?

Diabetes UK explains that HbA1c is glycated haemoglobin. It forms when glucose in your blood sticks to your red blood cells.

Red blood cells are active for around 2 to 3 months, which is why the result reflects your average blood sugar over that time. That’s different from a finger-prick test, which Diabetes UK describes as a snapshot of your blood sugar at one moment.

The NHS uses the HbA1c test both to diagnose type 2 diabetes and to monitor type 1 or type 2 diabetes once it has been diagnosed.

What do HbA1c results mean?

Results are usually given in mmol/mol (millimoles per mole), but the NHS says they’re sometimes given as a percentage. Here’s how the NHS describes the ranges:

HbA1c result If you do not have diabetes If you have diabetes
Below 42mmol/mol (6%) Normal No separate wording given
42 to 47mmol/mol (6% to 6.5%) You may be at risk of getting diabetes (sometimes called prediabetes) Your diabetes is well controlled
48mmol/mol (6.5%) or above You may have diabetes Your doctor may review your treatment

Below 42mmol/mol (6%) (if you do not have diabetes Normal): no separate wording given

42 to 47mmol/mol (6% to 6.5%) (if you do not have diabetes You may be at risk of getting diabetes (sometimes called prediabetes)): your diabetes is well controlled

48mmol/mol (6.5%) or above (if you do not have diabetes You may have diabetes): your doctor may review your treatment

The NHS stresses that these levels are a guide. You may have agreed a different target with your care team, and results can be affected by other conditions or medicines.

If you’re in the at-risk range, our guide to what prediabetes is explains more.

What is a good HbA1c target if you have diabetes?

Diabetes UK says that for people with diabetes, an ideal HbA1c is 48mmol/mol (6.5%) or below. For people at risk of type 2 diabetes, it gives a target of below 42mmol/mol (6%).

Your target is personal, though. Diabetes UK says your healthcare team may set an individual target for you, and may aim to bring your level down in stages. For some older people, targets may be set higher because of the risk of a fall linked to low blood sugar.

The NHS notes that if diabetes isn’t well controlled, it can raise the risk of problems such as eye, kidney and nerve problems. That’s why it’s worth knowing your number and talking it through with your team.

How is the HbA1c test done?

The NHS describes it as a standard blood test:

  1. You don’t need to prepare. You can eat and drink as normal beforehand.
  2. A healthcare professional takes a small amount of blood, usually from the inside of your elbow.
  3. You may get a little bruising or swelling, which should go away after a few days.
  4. Results usually come back after a few days. If you haven’t heard anything after a few weeks, contact the GP surgery or specialist who arranged the test.

You may also be able to see your results in the NHS App.

How often should you have an HbA1c test?

The NHS says people with diabetes are usually advised to have an HbA1c test every 3 to 6 months. Diabetes UK says you’re entitled to one at least once a year.

Diabetes UK adds that some people need it more often, for example if they’re planning a baby, changing treatment or having problems managing their levels. If you haven’t had an HbA1c test in over a year, it says to contact your healthcare team.

Writing your results down, for example in a diary, can help you spot trends over time, Diabetes UK suggests.

What can affect your HbA1c result?

Diabetes UK lists several things that can change your HbA1c:

  • being unwell
  • some medicines, such as steroids
  • changes to your lifestyle
  • feeling very stressed or depressed

Some conditions can also make the result less accurate, including haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia. If any of these apply to you, Diabetes UK suggests asking your doctor whether a different test would be more accurate.

What happens if your HbA1c is high?

If you haven’t been diagnosed with diabetes, the NHS says you may need another test to confirm the result. Either way, it says you may be advised to make lifestyle changes, such as getting more exercise, losing weight and changing your diet, and you may be offered medicine or changes to your current treatment.

Diabetes UK’s suggestions for bringing HbA1c down include:

  1. Getting active. It says exercise can specifically help to bring down HbA1c levels.
  2. Eating a healthy, balanced diet.
  3. Stopping smoking, as smoking makes it harder for blood to flow around your body.
  4. Going on a local diabetes education course.
  5. Reviewing your treatment with your healthcare team.

Don’t change any medicine or insulin on your own. Talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian about what your result means and what to do next. If you’re starting with food, our low GI foods list is a practical place to begin.

Keeping track of what you eat

Your HbA1c reflects your blood sugar over 2 to 3 months, and Diabetes UK lists a healthy, balanced diet among the ways to help bring it down. If a meal has no label, the Dietary Insight app can estimate its sugar, salt and fat from a photo and suggest a healthier swap. It gives an estimate, so use it alongside your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Plantain and Blood Sugar: How to Enjoy It with Diabetes
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Plantain is a starchy food that Diabetes UK lists as low GI, but portion and cooking still matter. UK tips, recipe figures and healthier ways to cook it. How does plantain affect blood sugar? Plantain is a starchy food, so it raises blood sugar like other carbohydrates, but Diabetes UK lists it as an example of a low GI food that raises blood sugar slowly.
item.content:encoded:
How does plantain affect blood sugar? Plantain is a starchy food, so it raises blood sugar like other carbohydrates, but Diabetes UK lists it as an example of a low GI food that raises blood sugar slowly. Your portion size and how you cook it matter more than the GI on its own, so plantain can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes.

Is plantain a starchy food?

Yes. Diabetes UK says starchy foods are things like potatoes, rice, pasta, bread, chapattis, naan and plantain. Starchy foods contain carbohydrate, and the GI ranks carbohydrate foods by how quickly they raise your blood sugar.

That doesn’t mean you need to avoid plantain. Diabetes UK says to try to have some starchy foods every day, and notes that some starchy foods can raise blood glucose levels quickly, so it’s worth choosing lower-GI options where you can.

What is the GI of plantain?

The glycaemic index (GI) ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 by how quickly they raise blood sugar. Diabetes UK groups foods like this:

GI score What it means
55 or below Low: raises blood sugar slowly
56 to 69 Medium: raises blood sugar at a medium rate
70 or more High: raises blood sugar quickly

55 or below: Low: raises blood sugar slowly

56 to 69: Medium: raises blood sugar at a medium rate

70 or more: High: raises blood sugar quickly

Diabetes UK includes plantain and yam in its list of example low GI foods. By comparison, it lists regular potatoes, whether baked, boiled, fried or mashed, as high GI. For more examples, see our low GI foods list.

Diabetes UK also lists plantain as a lower-GI swap. It suggests choosing brown or basmati rice instead of white rice, or trying plantain, quinoa, bulgur wheat or barley for a change.

Does ripeness or cooking change how plantain affects blood sugar?

The GI of a food isn’t fixed. Diabetes UK says several things can change it, including:

  1. The ripeness or variety of fruit and vegetables.
  2. Cooking methods, such as frying, boiling and baking.
  3. Processing, such as milling or pureeing.
  4. Fat and protein, which both lower the GI of a food.

So green plantain and very ripe plantain may not behave in exactly the same way, and boiled, steamed, baked or fried plantain may differ too. Diabetes UK doesn’t give separate GI figures for each one, so it’s best not to rely on a single number.

A lower GI isn’t the whole story. Diabetes UK points out that crisps have a lower GI than potatoes cooked without fat, because fat lowers the GI. That’s why the oil you use still matters.

Is the amount of plantain more important than the GI?

Yes. Diabetes UK says the amount of carbs you eat has a bigger effect on blood sugar levels than GI alone. GI also doesn’t take your portion size into account.

Diabetes UK’s advice is that the most important thing is to watch your carbohydrate portion sizes. It also notes that larger portions can make it more difficult to manage your weight.

A few practical ways to do this with plantain:

  1. Serve it as one part of the plate, not the whole meal.
  2. Pair it with beans, fish, chicken or eggs. Diabetes UK says protein, fat and fibre slow down the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates.
  3. Add vegetables or a salsa on the side for extra fibre.
  4. If you’re having plantain with rice, think about the total amount of starchy food on the plate.

If you’d like help working out the right amount of carbohydrate for you, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

What are healthier ways to cook plantain?

Fried plantain, often called dodo, is a favourite in many homes. The UK recipes below show other ways to enjoy it using little or no oil.

Recipe How it’s cooked Oil used
Diabetes UK plantain chips Thinly sliced green plantain, baked 2 tsp sunflower oil for 4 servings
NHS grilled plantain with fresh salsa Ripe plantain, grilled None listed
NHS ewa oloyin with plantain Ripe plantain, steamed 2 tsp vegetable oil for the whole dish

Diabetes UK plantain chips (how it’s cooked Thinly sliced green plantain, baked): 2 tsp sunflower oil for 4 servings

NHS grilled plantain with fresh salsa (how it’s cooked Ripe plantain, grilled): none listed

NHS ewa oloyin with plantain (how it’s cooked Ripe plantain, steamed): 2 tsp vegetable oil for the whole dish

When you do use oil, Diabetes UK lists olive oil, vegetable oil and rapeseed oil as healthier fats. It describes butter, palm nut oil and coconut oil as less healthy options.

What’s in a serving of these plantain recipes?

Here are the per-serving figures from each recipe page. Each recipe serves 4.

item.title: Jollof Rice and Diabetes: Healthier Swaps for a UK Kitchen
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Yes, you can still enjoy jollof rice with diabetes. Try brown basmati, a reduced-salt stock cube, less oil and more veg. Simple UK swaps and portion tips. Can you eat jollof rice with diabetes? Yes. Jollof rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes, and a few swaps make a real difference: brown basmati instead of white rice, a reduced-salt stock cube, a measured spoon of oil, plenty of vegetables and a sensible portion.
item.content:encoded:
Can you eat jollof rice with diabetes? Yes. Jollof rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes, and a few swaps make a real difference: brown basmati instead of white rice, a reduced-salt stock cube, a measured spoon of oil, plenty of vegetables and a sensible portion. Diabetes UK even has its own jollof rice and chicken recipe built around these ideas.

Why does jollof rice affect blood sugar?

Rice is a starchy food, and starchy foods are mostly carbohydrate. Diabetes UK lists rice alongside potatoes, pasta, bread, chapattis and plantain as starchy foods.

Diabetes UK says the amount of carbs you eat has a bigger effect on blood sugar levels than the glycaemic index (GI) alone. So the size of your portion matters most, followed by the type of rice you choose.

That doesn’t mean jollof is off the menu. The NHS calls rice and grains an excellent choice of starchy food, and suggests choosing wholegrain varieties where you can. For more on rice in general, see our guide is rice bad for diabetes?

Which rice is best for jollof if you have diabetes?

Diabetes UK suggests choosing brown rice or basmati rice instead of white rice. Brown basmati is a wholegrain, and wholegrains add fibre, which Diabetes UK says acts as a physical barrier that slows down the absorption of carbohydrate.

Diabetes UK groups foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar:

GI score What it means
55 or below Raises blood sugar slowly
56 to 69 Raises blood sugar at a medium rate
70 or more Raises blood sugar quickly

55 or below: Raises blood sugar slowly

56 to 69: Raises blood sugar at a medium rate

70 or more: Raises blood sugar quickly

Diabetes UK also notes that protein and fat lower the GI of a food. That’s one reason a jollof cooked with chicken, fish or beans and plenty of vegetables is a better choice than a large plate of rice on its own.

If you usually cook with easy-cook white rice, NHS Healthier Families says you could use easy-cook brown rice instead, but it will take an extra 10 to 15 minutes to cook. Keep an eye on the liquid as it simmers.

What are the best healthier jollof swaps?

These swaps come from the Diabetes UK and NHS jollof recipes and their wider healthy eating advice.

Instead of Try Why it helps
Long grain white rice Brown basmati rice Diabetes UK suggests brown or basmati rice instead of white
A regular stock cube A reduced-salt stock cube The NHS suggests low or reduced-salt stock cubes to cut salt
Free-pouring oil 2 tsp rapeseed oil for 4 servings Diabetes UK lists rapeseed oil as a healthier fat; its recipe uses 2 tsp
Extra salt Garlic, ginger, Scotch bonnet and herbs The NHS suggests herbs, spices, black pepper, garlic, chilli or lemon juice instead of salt
Rice on its own Peppers, okra and tomatoes cooked in More vegetables towards your 5 A Day
Fatty cuts of meat Chicken breast, fish, prawns or tofu Diabetes UK’s recipe uses chicken breast and suggests other options

Salt is worth watching because stock cubes and seasoning add up fast. The NHS says adults should have no more than 6g of salt a day, around 1 level teaspoon. Our guide to how much salt a day explains where hidden salt comes from.

What does a healthier serving of jollof look like?

Diabetes UK’s jollof rice and chicken recipe serves 4. It uses brown basmati rice, rapeseed oil, a reduced-salt chicken stock cube, chicken breast, peppers, tomatoes and okra. Here is the nutrition for each 393g serving, as given by Diabetes UK:

Fat 5.1g

Diabetes UK suggests you could make it with lamb, beef, pork or turkey instead of chicken. For a vegetarian or vegan version, it suggests courgette, aubergine and marinated tofu. For a seafood version, it suggests a fish stock cube with salmon or prawns.

How much jollof rice should you eat?

There’s no single right portion for everyone. Diabetes UK points out that portion sizes have grown as the plates and bowls we use have got bigger, and larger portions can make it more difficult to manage your weight.

A few practical ways to keep portions in check:

  1. Remember the NHS guide that starchy foods should make up just over a third of the food you eat, so rice doesn’t need to fill the whole plate.
  2. Serve jollof with grilled chicken, fish or meat and some brightly coloured steamed vegetables or a side salad, as NHS Healthier Families suggests.
  3. Add frozen vegetables to the pan towards the end of cooking, another NHS Healthier Families tip, to bulk out each portion.
  4. Use a smaller plate or bowl, since bigger plates have helped portions grow.

If you’d like help working out the right amount of rice or carbohydrate for you, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

Why does this matter for African and Caribbean communities?

Diabetes UK describes jollof as a popular West African dish, and a healthier version is easy to share with the whole household. Diabetes UK says people from Black African, African Caribbean and South Asian backgrounds are at risk of developing type 2 diabetes from the age of 25, much younger than the white population, whose risk increases from 40.

Diabetes UK also says carrying extra weight is the biggest risk factor for type 2 diabetes. It suggests making healthier food choices, such as eating more fruit and vegetables and choosing wholegrains.

How do you store and reheat leftover jollof safely?

Jollof often feeds a crowd, so leftovers are common. The NHS warns that if cooked rice or grains are left standing at room temperature, spores can germinate. The NHS also says rice should not be reheated more than once. After that, it should be thrown away.

item.title: How Much Sugar a Day? UK Limits for Adults and Children
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day, about 7 cubes, says the NHS. See UK limits by age, what counts and how to spot sugar on labels. How much sugar a day is OK in the UK? The NHS says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day, roughly 7 sugar cubes. Free sugars should make up no more than 5% of the energy (calories) you get from food and drink, and children’s limits are lower.
item.content:encoded:
How much sugar a day is OK in the UK? The NHS says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day, roughly 7 sugar cubes. Free sugars should make up no more than 5% of the energy (calories) you get from food and drink, and children’s limits are lower.

What counts as free sugars?

The daily limit applies to free sugars, not to every gram of sugar in your food. The NHS says free sugars include:

  • Any sugar added to food or drinks, such as in biscuits, chocolate, flavoured yoghurts, breakfast cereals and fizzy drinks.
  • Honey, syrups (such as maple, agave and golden syrup) and nectars.
  • Unsweetened fruit juices, vegetable juices and smoothies. The sugars in these occur naturally but still count as free sugars.

Sugar found naturally in milk, whole fruit and vegetables does not count as free sugars. The NHS says the sugar in fruit only becomes free sugar when the fruit is juiced or puréed.

How much sugar a day for adults and children?

These are the NHS maximum daily amounts of free sugars.

Age Maximum free sugars a day Roughly
Adults and children 11 and over 30g 7 sugar cubes
7 to 10 years 24g 6 sugar cubes
4 to 6 years 19g 5 sugar cubes
2 to 3 years 14g 3.5 sugar cubes
1 year 10g 2.5 sugar cubes

Adults and children 11 and over (maximum free sugars a day 30g): 7 sugar cubes

7 to 10 years (maximum free sugars a day 24g): 6 sugar cubes

4 to 6 years (maximum free sugars a day 19g): 5 sugar cubes

2 to 3 years (maximum free sugars a day 14g): 3.5 sugar cubes

1 year (maximum free sugars a day 10g): 2.5 sugar cubes

There’s no guideline limit for babies under 1, but the NHS says sugars should not be added to food or drinks given to babies.

NHS Healthier Families says children are having over 2 times more sugar than is recommended, with half of it coming from snacks and sugary drinks.

Why does too much sugar matter?

The NHS says eating too much sugar can make you gain weight and can also cause tooth decay. Sugar adds calories, and too many calories can lead to weight gain.

Being overweight raises your risk of health problems such as heart disease, some cancers and type 2 diabetes, according to the NHS. Sugar is also one of the main causes of tooth decay, which is why the NHS suggests keeping sugary foods to mealtimes.

How quickly does sugar add up?

Free sugars hide in everyday foods and drinks. Here are some examples from the NHS:

Food or drink Sugar
Can of cola Up to 9 cubes, more than the adult daily limit
Chocolate bar Up to 24g (6 cubes)
Sugary yoghurt pot Up to 24g (6 cubes)
Cereal bar 12g (3 cubes)
150ml glass of fruit juice Around 15g

Can of cola: Up to 9 cubes, more than the adult daily limit

Chocolate bar: Up to 24g (6 cubes)

Sugary yoghurt pot: Up to 24g (6 cubes)

Cereal bar: 12g (3 cubes)

150ml glass of fruit juice: Around 15g

Even unsweetened fruit juice and smoothies are sugary. The NHS says to keep them to a combined 150ml a day, drunk with a meal. They only count as one of your 5 A Day, however much you have. Our guide to what fruit diabetics can eat explains why whole fruit is the better choice.

How do you spot sugar on food labels?

The “of which sugars” figure on a label shows total sugars: free sugars plus the sugars from milk, fruit and vegetables. The NHS gives these guides per 100g:

  • High: more than 22.5g of total sugars per 100g.
  • Low: 5g of total sugars or less per 100g.
  • Medium: anything in between.

On front-of-pack labels, red means high, amber medium and green low. NHS Healthier Families suggests picking items with more greens and ambers and cutting down on ones with reds.

Because the label shows total sugars, some foods look higher than they are. The NHS says plain yoghurt may contain as much as 8g of sugar per serving, but none of it is free sugar.

The ingredients list helps too. The NHS says that if sugar is near the top of the list, the food is likely to be high in free sugars. The NHS says added sugar can appear under many names, including:

  1. Sucrose, glucose, fructose, dextrose and maltose.
  2. Cane sugar, brown sugar and crystalline sucrose.
  3. Corn syrup and high-fructose corn syrup.
  4. Honey, molasses and treacle.
  5. Maple syrup, agave syrup and nectars.
  6. Fruit juice concentrates and purées.

For more on reading the whole label, see our guide to reading food labels with diabetes.

What are easy ways to cut down on sugar?

The NHS suggests small swaps that add up:

  • Drink water, lower-fat milk, or sugar-free, diet or no-added-sugar drinks instead of sugary fizzy drinks or squash.
  • If you take sugar in hot drinks or add it to breakfast cereal, gradually reduce the amount.
  • Try sliced banana on toast in place of high-sugar spreads.
  • Choose unsweetened wholegrain breakfast cereals that are not frosted.
  • Buy tinned fruit in juice rather than syrup.
  • Try reducing the sugar in your recipes. The NHS says it works for most things except jam, meringues and ice cream.
  • Keep sweets and treats to mealtimes to help protect teeth.

If you have diabetes and want help with how sugar and carbohydrates fit into your meals, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

Checking meals without a label

Home-cooked meals, takeaways and restaurant dishes rarely come with a label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a healthier swap. It gives an estimate, so use it alongside food labels and your healthcare team’s advice.
