item.title: Foods That Can Help Lower Blood Pressure: A UK Guide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Which foods can help lower blood pressure? Fruit, veg, wholegrains, low-fat dairy and less salt. A plain-English UK list with portions and what to limit. Foods that can help lower blood pressure include fruit and vegetables, wholegrains such as oats, lean protein and low-fat dairy, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF).
item.content:encoded:
Foods that can help lower blood pressure include fruit and vegetables, wholegrains such as oats, lean protein and low-fat dairy, according to the British Heart Foundation (BHF). What you cut back on matters just as much: less salt, less alcohol and fewer sugary, fatty foods. No single food does the job, but the overall pattern of your plate can make a real difference.

Why does food make a difference to blood pressure?

The NHS lists an unhealthy diet, especially one that’s high in salt, as one of the things that raises your risk of high blood pressure. It also says healthy lifestyle changes can help lower your blood pressure, and that lowering it even a small amount can help reduce your risk of serious health problems.

The BHF describes diet as one of the tools you can use to help keep blood pressure under control. It sits alongside being active, not smoking, keeping to a healthy weight and taking any medicines you’ve been prescribed.

Which foods can help lower blood pressure?

Here’s a quick summary of the BHF’s advice on what to include more often.

Food group Examples Why it’s recommended
Fruit and vegetables Bananas, spinach, kale, celery, strawberries, beetroot Supply potassium, which can help lower blood pressure
Wholegrains Oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread Fibre; oat beta-glucans may help
Lean protein Chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, beans A swap for red and processed meats
Low-fat dairy Semi-skimmed milk, low-fat natural yogurt Calcium is linked to lower blood pressure

Fruit and vegetables (examples Bananas, spinach, kale, celery, strawberries, beetroot): supply potassium, which can help lower blood pressure

Wholegrains (examples Oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread): fibre; oat beta-glucans may help

Lean protein (examples Chicken, turkey, fish, eggs, beans): a swap for red and processed meats

Low-fat dairy (examples Semi-skimmed milk, low-fat natural yogurt): calcium is linked to lower blood pressure

Fruit and vegetables

The BHF says all fruit and vegetables supply potassium, which can help lower blood pressure, and suggests eating at least five portions every day. Blood Pressure UK says one portion is 80g.

Some vegetables also contain nitrates. The BHF says research has suggested beetroot juice might help lower blood pressure, and that spinach, celery, kale, bananas and strawberries are other sources of nitrates.

Wholegrains and fibre

Swap white versions for wholegrains such as brown rice, wholemeal bread and oats. The BHF says the soluble fibre in oats, called beta-glucans, may help in lowering blood pressure. Beans, lentils, nuts and seeds are good sources of fibre too.

Lean protein and low-fat dairy

The BHF suggests choosing chicken, turkey, fish, eggs and beans instead of red and processed meats. It also says milk and dairy could help with lowering blood pressure, as calcium is linked to blood pressure reduction. Semi-skimmed milk and low-fat natural yogurt are easy choices.

What counts as a portion of fruit and veg?

Blood Pressure UK gives these examples of one 80g portion:

  1. A small bowl of salad.
  2. Three heaped tablespoons of vegetables, or of beans and pulses.
  3. One medium fruit, or two smaller fruits.
  4. Two to three tablespoons of berries or grapes.
  5. One tablespoon of dried fruit, best eaten at mealtimes.
  6. A 150ml glass of fruit juice, which only counts once a day however much you drink.

Fresh, frozen, tinned and dried all count. Choose tinned fruit in juice or water, with no added sugar or salt. Potatoes, yams, cassava and plantain don’t count, but sweet potatoes, parsnips, swedes and turnips do.

If you’re managing blood sugar too, our guide to what fruit diabetics can eat covers portions and juice in more detail.

Which foods are rich in potassium?

Blood Pressure UK lists these potassium-rich foods:

  • Fruit: bananas, apricots, currants, orange juice, tomato juice and tomato purée.
  • Vegetables: potatoes, sweet potatoes, asparagus, spinach, cabbage and sprouts.
  • Other foods: salmon, tuna tinned in spring water, yogurt, fat-free milk, eggs, almonds, mushrooms and wholemeal pasta.

Get your potassium from food, not tablets. The BHF says too much potassium can affect the rhythm of the heart, and that this is especially dangerous for people with kidney problems or taking certain water tablets. Only take potassium supplements if your doctor has prescribed them.

Blood Pressure UK adds that if you have kidney disease or take certain blood pressure medicines, you should check with your doctor before greatly increasing the potassium in your diet. It also says to avoid potassium-based salt substitutes in that case. If you have diabetes or kidney problems, Blood Pressure UK says to check with your doctor or nurse before using a low-sodium salt substitute.

Which foods should you limit?

Salt

The BHF says we should have no more than 6g of salt a day, which is about a teaspoon. Much of it is hidden in everyday foods such as bread, breakfast cereals, sauces, crisps, olives, pickles and processed meats. Our guide to how much salt a day shows how to spot it on labels.

Alcohol

Too much alcohol can raise blood pressure. The BHF suggests staying well within the guideline of no more than 14 units a week, with some alcohol-free days.

Sugary and fatty foods

The BHF says sugar and fat may not directly affect blood pressure, but the weight gain they can cause is linked to raised blood pressure. For snacks, it suggests fruit, plain yogurt, nuts and dried fruit.

Caffeine

The BHF says a moderate intake, 4 to 5 cups a day, should not be a problem for most people. Coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate all contain caffeine.

For a full eating plan built around these foods, see our DASH diet UK guide.

Can food replace blood pressure medicine?

Don’t stop or change any medicine because you’ve changed what you eat. The BHF says it’s important to take any medicines you’ve been prescribed, and healthy eating works alongside them. If you have questions about your blood pressure or your treatment, talk to your GP, practice nurse or a dietitian.

When should you get help?

The NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if you often have headaches or blurred vision, have chest pain that comes and goes, or have other symptoms you’re worried could be caused by high blood pressure.

Call 999 if you get sudden chest pain or discomfort that does not go away, pain that spreads to your arms, neck, jaw, stomach or back, or chest pain with feeling sweaty, sick, light-headed or short of breath. The NHS says you could be having a heart attack. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

Checking the salt on your plate

When a meal doesn’t come with a label, the Dietary Insight app can estimate the salt, sugar and fat from a photo and suggest a lower-salt swap. It gives an estimate, so use it alongside food labels and your healthcare team’s advice.

item.title: Eating Out with a Food Allergy UK: What to Ask and Check
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Eating out with a food allergy in the UK? What restaurants must tell you, the questions to ask before you order, takeaway rules and when to call 999. Eating out with a food allergy in the UK starts with one rule: restaurants, cafés and takeaways must tell you if any of the 14 major allergens are in their food.
item.content:encoded:
Eating out with a food allergy in the UK starts with one rule: restaurants, cafés and takeaways must tell you if any of the 14 major allergens are in their food. The rest is up to you and the staff, so plan ahead, ask clear questions every time you order and carry your emergency medicine if you’ve been prescribed it.

What do UK restaurants have to tell you about allergens?

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says food businesses must tell you if they use any of the 14 regulated allergens as ingredients. Our guide to the 14 major food allergens explains what they are and where they hide.

The information can be on the menu, or the menu can tell you how to get it, for example by asking staff. For loose food, such as from a bakery or deli counter, the FSA says the business can tell you verbally, but it must signpost where the information can be found.

Anaphylaxis UK adds that businesses don’t have to publish a full ingredients list. They do need a system that gives accurate information for every item containing the 14 allergens.

What should you do before you book?

A little planning makes the meal itself much calmer. Anaphylaxis UK and Allergy UK both suggest you:

  1. Look at the menu online and pick one or two dishes that might suit you.
  2. Phone ahead, ideally speaking to a manager or head chef. Ask how the food is prepared and how they control cross-contamination.
  3. Ask whether the person you spoke to will be there when you eat.
  4. Choose a quieter time, such as early evening or a weekday. Allergy UK says chefs are more likely to make a mistake when the restaurant is busy.
  5. Think about the type of food. Both charities say seafood restaurants carry a higher risk for fish or shellfish allergy, and some Asian cuisines carry a higher risk for nut allergy.
  6. Avoid buffets and salad bars, where utensils are shared, unless you’re served first.

If the risks feel high on a particular occasion, Anaphylaxis UK says it may be best to bring your own food or eat somewhere else.

What should you ask staff when you order?

The NHS advises telling staff at restaurants and cafés about your allergy. Be clear and give examples of the foods that cause a reaction, the FSA suggests. Useful questions include:

Ask about Why it matters
Ingredients in the dish Allergens can be hidden in complicated recipes, the FSA says
Sauces, glazes, garnishes and cooking oil These can add allergens you wouldn’t expect
Recipe changes or substitutions Allergy UK says recipes can change without warning
Shared pans, griddles and fryers Anaphylaxis UK says woks and frying pans may not be cleaned thoroughly
Bread, rolls and desserts Rolls can contain nuts or seeds

Ingredients in the dish: Allergens can be hidden in complicated recipes, the FSA says

Sauces, glazes, garnishes and cooking oil: These can add allergens you wouldn’t expect

Recipe changes or substitutions: Allergy UK says recipes can change without warning

Shared pans, griddles and fryers: Anaphylaxis UK says woks and frying pans may not be cleaned thoroughly

Bread, rolls and desserts: Rolls can contain nuts or seeds

Anaphylaxis UK gives some examples of hidden allergens: sauces may contain wheat flour, and some curries may be thickened with peanut flour or ground almonds. Allergy UK suggests asking the chef to use clean pans, clean utensils and fresh oil.

Allergy UK lists simple dishes as lower-risk choices, such as plain grilled or roast meat without marinades or sauces, steamed vegetables and potatoes, and fresh fruit for dessert. Even then, ask about every part of the plate.

What if you’re not confident in the answers?

If staff don’t seem to understand your needs, the FSA says ask for the manager. If you still have doubts, the FSA’s advice is simple: do not eat there.

When your food arrives, check it again before eating. Allergy UK says to send it back if you see or smell an allergen, and to ask for a freshly made meal. Removing the ingredient from the same plate isn’t enough.

It’s also worth remembering that a dish you’ve eaten before isn’t automatically fine next time. Anaphylaxis UK points out that recipes vary between restaurants and even within the same one.

How do allergen rules work for takeaways and delivery?

The FSA says that when you order food at a distance, such as by phone or online, allergen information must be available to you at two stages: when you order, and when the food is delivered. If you’re ordering for several people, ask the business to label each meal and container.

Anaphylaxis UK recommends phoning the restaurant directly rather than relying on notes or messages passed on through apps. Our guide to healthy takeaway options has more tips on choosing what to order.

What should you take with you?

The NHS says to carry 2 adrenaline auto-injectors or nasal sprays with you at all times, if they’ve been prescribed for you. Anaphylaxis UK also suggests having an up-to-date allergy action plan. Both charities say at least one person you’re eating with should know about your allergy, and Allergy UK adds they should know how to use your device.

Anaphylaxis UK says alcohol, tiredness, infections and poorly treated asthma can raise the risk of a serious reaction, so factor these in when you plan a night out.

What should you do if you have a reaction?

Call 999 straight away if lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, breathing becomes fast or difficult, the throat feels tight or it’s hard to swallow, skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale, or someone becomes suddenly confused, drowsy or dizzy, or faints. These can be signs of anaphylaxis.

If you have an adrenaline auto-injector or nasal spray, the NHS says to use it immediately, then call 999 for an ambulance, even if you or the person you’re with seems to feel better. Do not drive yourself to A&E. Anaphylaxis UK adds: tell someone straight away, stay where you are and follow your emergency plan.

If you think you may have a food allergy that hasn’t been diagnosed, the NHS says to see a GP. If a business didn’t meet the allergen rules, the FSA says you can report it to the local authority.

Checking a dish before you ask

Before you order, the Dietary Insight app can flag ingredients in a photo of a dish that may contain allergens on your profile, which can give you a starting point for your questions. It can’t see hidden ingredients or cross-contamination, so always ask staff and check the full label.

item.title: What Fruit Can Diabetics Eat? A UK Guide to Portions and Juice
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: People with diabetes can eat any fruit they like, says Diabetes UK. See UK portion sizes, why juice is limited to 150ml and how to spread fruit across the day. What fruit can diabetics eat? Any fruit you like. Diabetes UK says there’s no reason people with diabetes can’t eat any fruit, as long as it’s whole fruit spread through the day.
item.content:encoded:
What fruit can diabetics eat? Any fruit you like. Diabetes UK says there’s no reason people with diabetes can’t eat any fruit, as long as it’s whole fruit spread through the day. The things that matter most are portion size, keeping dried fruit small and limiting fruit juice and smoothies to 150ml a day.

Can people with diabetes eat fruit?

Yes. Diabetes UK puts it plainly: having diabetes doesn’t mean you can’t have fruit. Fresh, frozen, dried and tinned fruit all count towards your 5 A Day.

Fruit gives you fibre, which Diabetes UK says is good for your overall health. It does also contain carbohydrate in the form of sugar, and that affects your blood glucose levels. That’s why how much you eat in one go matters more than which fruit you choose.

Is the sugar in fruit bad for diabetes?

The sugar in whole fruit is treated differently from the sugar in biscuits or fizzy drinks. Diabetes UK says the sugar naturally found in whole fruit does not count towards free sugar, because your body uses it differently.

Diabetes UK also notes that most fruits have a low to medium glycaemic index (GI). That means they don’t have the same immediate effect on blood sugar as refined carbs like white bread. If you want to know more about GI, our low GI foods list explains how it works.

Juice is a different story, and we cover it below.

Which fruits are best for diabetes?

There’s no list of banned fruits. Diabetes UK’s advice covers any fruit you like, including bananas, grapes, mango and pineapple. Instead of picking “good” and “bad” fruits, focus on these three things:

  1. Choose whole fruit over juice. Whole fruit keeps its fibre. Juice loses most of it.
  2. Watch the portion. Diabetes UK says it’s easy to overdo it if you eat a whole bowl. A portion is roughly what fits in the palm of your hand.
  3. Spread it out. Have your fruit across the day rather than several portions in one sitting.

How big is a portion of fruit?

The NHS says one adult portion of fruit is 80g of fresh, tinned or frozen fruit, or 30g of dried fruit. Here are some everyday examples from the NHS and Diabetes UK.

Type of fruit One portion looks like
Small fruit 2 plums, 2 satsumas, 2 kiwi fruit, 3 apricots, 7 strawberries or 14 cherries
Medium fruit 1 apple, banana, pear, orange or nectarine
Large fruit Half a grapefruit, 1 slice of melon (5cm), 1 large slice of pineapple or 2 slices of mango (5cm)
Grapes 1 handful
Tinned fruit 2 pear or peach halves, or 2 pineapple rings in natural juice
Frozen fruit 2 handfuls (4 heaped tablespoons) of frozen blueberries
Dried fruit 1 heaped tablespoon of raisins or sultanas, 2 figs, 3 prunes or 2 Medjool dates

Small fruit: 2 plums, 2 satsumas, 2 kiwi fruit, 3 apricots, 7 strawberries or 14 cherries

Medium fruit: 1 apple, banana, pear, orange or nectarine

Large fruit: Half a grapefruit, 1 slice of melon (5cm), 1 large slice of pineapple or 2 slices of mango (5cm)

Grapes: 1 handful

Tinned fruit: 2 pear or peach halves, or 2 pineapple rings in natural juice

Frozen fruit: 2 handfuls (4 heaped tablespoons) of frozen blueberries

Dried fruit: 1 heaped tablespoon of raisins or sultanas, 2 figs, 3 prunes or 2 Medjool dates

Diabetes UK says these portion sizes are a guide based on an average healthy adult. Your dietitian can advise you on portions that are right for you.

What about dried fruit?

Dried fruit counts towards your 5 A Day, but the portion is small. Diabetes UK says a portion is just one tablespoon, so it’s easy to eat several without noticing.

The NHS adds that dried fruit can be high in sugar and can be bad for your teeth. It recommends eating dried fruit at mealtimes, for example as part of a dessert, rather than as a snack between meals.

Can diabetics drink fruit juice and smoothies?

You can, but keep it small. The NHS says to limit fruit juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml a day, which is one small glass, and Diabetes UK gives the same 150ml limit.

There are a few reasons for this:

  • It counts as free sugar. Diabetes UK says the sugar in fruit juice and smoothies counts towards your free sugar intake, unlike whole fruit.
  • There’s less fibre. Juice doesn’t contain as much fibre as the fruit itself, and Diabetes UK says it’s easy to drink too much in a short time, which can raise blood glucose levels.
  • It only counts once. The NHS says unsweetened juice and smoothies can only ever count as one portion of your 5 A Day, however much you drink.

Watch out for drinks labelled “juice drink”. The NHS says these are unlikely to count towards your 5 A Day, and Diabetes UK warns that some smoothies and juice drinks have extra sugar added, so read the ingredients.

Is tinned and frozen fruit OK?

Yes. Both count towards your 5 A Day, and frozen fruit is handy for porridge or yoghurt.

With tinned fruit, the NHS and Diabetes UK both say to choose fruit tinned in natural juice rather than syrup. Always check the label to be sure there’s no added sugar.

Simple ways to fit fruit into your day

  • Add a handful of berries to porridge or plain yoghurt at breakfast.
  • Have an apple, pear or two satsumas as a snack instead of biscuits. Our best snacks for type 2 diabetes has more ideas.
  • Keep frozen fruit in the freezer so you always have some in.
  • Choose a whole orange over a glass of orange juice.
  • Keep dried fruit for mealtimes, such as a spoonful on cereal.

If you take medication for diabetes or have been given a specific eating plan, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian before making big changes to your diet.

Checking meals without a label

Fruit is easy to spot, but the sugar in a fruit salad, smoothie or dessert when you’re eating out is harder to judge. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap, which can help you see where most of the sugar on your plate comes from.

item.title: Type 2 Diabetes Symptoms: Signs to Look Out For in the UK
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Type 2 diabetes symptoms include tiredness, peeing more, thirst and weight loss, but many people have none. Learn the signs, risks and when to see a GP. Type 2 diabetes symptoms most often include feeling very tired, peeing more than usual, feeling thirsty all the time and losing weight without trying.
item.content:encoded:
Type 2 diabetes symptoms most often include feeling very tired, peeing more than usual, feeling thirsty all the time and losing weight without trying. They may come on gradually, and many people have no symptoms at all, so the NHS says it’s important to get checked if you think you’re at risk.

What are the most common symptoms of type 2 diabetes?

The NHS lists four main symptoms:

  1. Feeling very tired
  2. Peeing more than usual
  3. Feeling thirsty all the time
  4. Losing weight without trying to

Other symptoms the NHS mentions are blurred vision, cuts or wounds taking longer to heal, and itching around the penis or vagina, or getting thrush again and again. The NHS says these symptoms are the same for adults and children.

What are the 4 Ts of diabetes?

Diabetes UK uses the 4 Ts as an easy way to remember the main signs of diabetes:

The T What it means
Toilet Going for a wee a lot, especially at night
Thirsty Being really thirsty
Tired Feeling more tired than usual
Thinner Losing weight without trying to

Toilet: Going for a wee a lot, especially at night

Thirsty: Being really thirsty

Tired: Feeling more tired than usual

Thinner: Losing weight without trying to

Diabetes UK also lists increased hunger, behaviour changes such as feeling more irritable, genital itching or thrush, cuts and wounds taking longer to heal, and blurred eyesight. It explains that these symptoms happen when there isn’t enough insulin to move glucose (sugar) from the blood into the cells.

Having some of these symptoms doesn’t mean you definitely have diabetes, Diabetes UK says. But it is a good reason to speak to your GP.

Can you have type 2 diabetes without knowing?

Yes, and this is one of the most important things to know. The NHS says not everyone with type 2 diabetes has symptoms, and when symptoms do appear they may develop gradually.

Diabetes UK says type 2 diabetes can be easier to miss because it develops more slowly, especially in the early stages. It can go undiagnosed for years if you don’t have symptoms or your symptoms are missed.

That’s why knowing your risk matters as much as knowing the symptoms. If you’ve been told you have raised blood sugar, our guide to what prediabetes is explains what that means.

Who is more likely to get type 2 diabetes?

The NHS says you’re more likely to get type 2 diabetes if:

  • you’re white and over 40, or over 25 and from a South Asian, Chinese, Black African or Black Caribbean background
  • a parent, brother or sister has it
  • you’re overweight and not very physically active
  • you have a condition that increases your risk, such as high blood pressure

Diabetes UK adds that people from African Caribbean, Black African or South Asian backgrounds are at higher risk, often from a younger age. It also lists your waist measurement and genetics among the risk factors, and says risk increases as you get older.

Type 2 diabetes doesn’t only affect people living with overweight or obesity, Diabetes UK says, although that is one of the risk factors.

How do I check if I have type 2 diabetes?

The NHS suggests using Diabetes UK’s free Know Your Risk tool, which Diabetes UK says takes about two minutes. If your score is high or very high, Diabetes UK says you’ll need to ask your GP for a blood test.

If you’re between 40 and 74 and don’t have an existing health condition, the NHS says you may also be able to get a free NHS Health Check at your GP surgery or a local pharmacy.

Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with a blood test that checks how high your blood glucose levels are. The NHS says results usually take a few days.

When should you see a GP?

The NHS says to see a GP if you think you or your child may have type 2 diabetes, or if you or your child have a higher risk of getting it.

Diabetes UK says that if you feel very unwell, or your symptoms of diabetes have come on quickly, it’s essential to make an urgent appointment with your GP or call NHS 111.

When to call 999

The NHS high blood sugar page says to call 999 or go to A&E if you think you have high blood sugar and:

  • you’re feeling sick, being sick or have stomach pain
  • you’re breathing more quickly than usual or your heart is beating faster than usual
  • you feel drowsy or are struggling to stay awake
  • your breath has a fruity smell (like pear drop sweets)
  • you feel confused or have difficulty concentrating
  • you have a high level of ketones in your blood or pee

The NHS says these could be signs you’re becoming seriously unwell. Don’t drive yourself to A&E: ask someone to drive you, or call 999 for an ambulance.

Why getting diagnosed early matters

Diabetes UK says untreated diabetes can harm many major organs, including the heart, blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys. It adds that being diagnosed early and managing your blood sugar levels can help prevent these complications.

If you’ve already been diagnosed and have questions about your treatment, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

Keeping an eye on everyday meals

Once you know your risk, small food choices add up. Our low GI foods list is a good place to start. When a meal has no label, the Dietary Insight app can estimate its sugar, salt and fat from a photo and suggest a swap.

item.title: Healthy Takeaway Options for Diabetes: A UK Menu Guide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Healthy takeaway options for diabetes: what to order from the curry house, chippy, pizza place, Chinese, Thai and kebab shop, with simple UK swaps. Healthy takeaway options for diabetes usually come down to three things: how the food is cooked, what you have on the side and how big the portion is. Grilled, baked, steamed and tomato-based dishes are generally better choices than fried or creamy ones, and swapping fried rice, naan or a large portion of chips for plainer sides can help too.
item.content:encoded:
Healthy takeaway options for diabetes usually come down to three things: how the food is cooked, what you have on the side and how big the portion is. Grilled, baked, steamed and tomato-based dishes are generally better choices than fried or creamy ones, and swapping fried rice, naan or a large portion of chips for plainer sides can help too.

Can you eat takeaways with diabetes?

Yes. Diabetes UK says having diabetes shouldn’t stop you enjoying eating out. Its tips are about choosing portion sizes, toppings and sides carefully.

It helps to know where the fat and salt hide. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) says most shop-bought or restaurant pizzas are high in saturated fat and can be salty too, and that a chicken korma is likely to be high in saturated fat and potentially salt.

The NHS says the average man should eat no more than 30g of saturated fat a day and the average woman no more than 20g, so it is worth knowing which dishes are richest.

What to order: a quick UK takeaway guide

Here are the swaps suggested by Diabetes UK, the NHS and the BHF for the most common takeaways.

Takeaway Better choices Go easy on
Indian Tandoori or tikka dishes, dry or tomato-based curries such as madras, boiled rice, chapatti or roti Creamy curries such as korma, pasanda or masala, pilau rice, naan, poppadoms
Chinese Steamed fish, chicken chop suey, szechuan prawns, broth-based soups, steamed rice Fried rice, spring rolls, satays
Thai Stir-fried or steamed dishes with chicken, fish or veg, Thai salad, broth-based soups Coconut milk curries (leave some of the sauce)
Fish and chips A smaller portion, thick-cut chips, mushy peas, grilled fish if they offer it Extra salt, crinkle-cut or curly fries
Pizza Thin base, vegetable, chicken or seafood toppings, a side salad, sharing Extra cheese, pepperoni, salami, bacon
Burger Lean or veggie burger, extra salad, bun-less for fewer carbs Cheese, mayonnaise, creamy dressings
Kebab Shish kebab with pitta and salad Doner kebab

Indian (better choices Tandoori or tikka dishes, dry or tomato-based curries such as madras, boiled rice, chapatti or roti): creamy curries such as korma, pasanda or masala, pilau rice, naan, poppadoms

Chinese (better choices Steamed fish, chicken chop suey, szechuan prawns, broth-based soups, steamed rice): fried rice, spring rolls, satays

Thai (better choices Stir-fried or steamed dishes with chicken, fish or veg, Thai salad, broth-based soups): coconut milk curries (leave some of the sauce)

Fish and chips (better choices A smaller portion, thick-cut chips, mushy peas, grilled fish if they offer it): extra salt, crinkle-cut or curly fries

Pizza (better choices Thin base, vegetable, chicken or seafood toppings, a side salad, sharing): extra cheese, pepperoni, salami, bacon

Burger (better choices Lean or veggie burger, extra salad, bun-less for fewer carbs): cheese, mayonnaise, creamy dressings

Kebab (better choices Shish kebab with pitta and salad): doner kebab

How to order a healthier Indian takeaway

Diabetes UK suggests tandoori and tikka options because they are baked and lower in fat. The NHS also recommends dry or tomato-based dishes, such as tandoori or madras, instead of creamy curries like korma, pasanda or masala.

For sides, choose boiled or steamed rice rather than pilau or fried rice, and wholemeal chapatti or roti rather than naan. Diabetes UK points out that naans are often very large, made with low-fibre white flour and may have a lot of butter.

Diabetes UK has a simple plate tip: fill your plate with salad and a portion of unsweetened yoghurt first, then add rice to the space that’s left. Dhal is rich in fibre but can be quite oily, so sharing a portion works well. Our guide is rice bad for diabetes has more on rice portions.

What about Chinese and Thai takeaways?

The NHS suggests lower-fat Chinese dishes such as steamed fish, chicken chop suey or szechuan prawns. Diabetes UK recommends broth-based soups or a Thai salad as a starter rather than spring rolls or satays, with dressings and dips served on the side.

Diabetes UK also suggests steamed or fragrant basmati rice rather than fried rice.

For Thai food, the NHS says to try stir-fried or steamed dishes with chicken, fish or vegetables. Curries made with coconut milk are high in saturated fat, so if you choose one, try not to eat all the sauce.

Fish and chips, pizza and burgers

Fish and chips: Diabetes UK suggests ordering a smaller portion and removing the batter from the fish. Go for thick-cut chips, because the thicker the chip, the less fat it absorbs. The BHF adds that you can ask them to hold the salt, mushy peas add fibre, and some chip shops will grill your fish if you ask.

Pizza: Diabetes UK recommends a thin base, sharing a pizza and filling up on a side salad. The BHF says cheese and meaty toppings like salami, pepperoni, ham and bacon are the main sources of saturated fat and salt, and the NHS suggests lower-fat toppings such as vegetables, chicken, tuna or other seafood instead.

Burgers: try the lean or veggie option and leave out the cheese and mayonnaise. Diabetes UK says going bun-less is a lower carb option, and you can ask for extra lettuce, tomatoes and gherkins, though it’s worth watching the dressing.

Kebabs: the NHS suggests a shish kebab with pitta bread and salad rather than a doner.

Simple habits that help with any takeaway

  1. Check the calories. Diabetes UK says restaurants, cafes and takeaways that employ more than 250 people have to show calories on their menus, which makes comparing dishes easier.
  2. Watch the extras. Diabetes UK says to watch out for extras such as poppadoms and naan, and suggests soups, veg sticks with dips, chicken tikka or grilled fish as healthier starters than spring rolls, samosas and pakoras.
  3. Swap the drink. Choose a sugar-free drink rather than a sugary one. Diabetes UK says plain water is best.
  4. Share rich dishes. Diabetes UK suggests sharing a pizza or a portion of dhal to help manage portion sizes.
  5. Fit in a walk. Diabetes UK suggests a brisk walk before or after the meal to help keep blood sugar levels stable.

For more on cutting back on salt, see our guide to how much salt a day.

If you use insulin

Diabetes UK notes that estimating the carbs in a restaurant or takeaway meal is harder than usual, because you don’t know exactly how the dish was made. It also says dishes such as pizza, curry and fried fish and chips may take hours to affect your blood glucose levels.

If you use insulin or other diabetes medication, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian about how to plan for takeaways and meals out.

Checking a takeaway without a label

Most takeaways don’t come with a nutrition label. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap, which can help when you’re deciding what to order next time.

item.title: Low GI Foods List UK: What to Eat for Steadier Blood Sugar
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Low GI foods (55 or below) raise blood sugar slowly. See a UK list of low, medium and high GI foods, what changes GI, and why portion size matters more. Low GI foods are carbohydrate foods with a glycaemic index of 55 or below, so they raise blood sugar slowly. A UK low GI foods list includes most fruit and veg, beans, lentils, steel-cut oats, rye bread, yam, plantain and unsweetened milk and yoghurt.
item.content:encoded:
Low GI foods are carbohydrate foods with a glycaemic index of 55 or below, so they raise blood sugar slowly. A UK low GI foods list includes most fruit and veg, beans, lentils, steel-cut oats, rye bread, yam, plantain and unsweetened milk and yoghurt. GI is a useful tool, but the amount of carbohydrate you eat matters even more.

What is the glycaemic index?

The glycaemic index (GI) ranks carbohydrate foods and drinks on a scale of 0 to 100 by how quickly they raise blood sugar. Diabetes UK uses three bands:

  • Low GI: 55 or below, raises blood sugar slowly
  • Medium GI: 56 to 69, raises blood sugar at a moderate rate
  • High GI: 70 or more, raises blood sugar quickly

Only foods that contain carbohydrate have a GI. The British Dietetic Association (BDA) notes that carbs from starchy foods and from added and natural sugars all raise blood glucose.

Which foods are low, medium and high GI?

Here are examples from Diabetes UK’s lists. Values can vary between brands and with how food is cooked, so treat this as a rough guide.

Low GI (55 or below) Medium GI (56 to 69) High GI (70 or more)
Apples, pears, oranges, grapes and most berries Pineapple, cantaloupe melon and overripe bananas Watermelon
Dried apricots Sweet potato, pumpkin and parsnip Potatoes, whether baked, boiled, fried or mashed
Carrots, tomatoes, spinach, broccoli and mushrooms New potatoes and broad beans White bread and some wholemeal breads
Beans, peas and lentils Basmati rice and couscous Bagels and doughnuts
Steel-cut oats and rye bread Chapatti Some sugary breakfast cereals
Yam and plantain Plain popcorn Sweets and sugary drinks
Unsweetened milk and yoghurt

Apples, pears, oranges, grapes and most berries (medium gi (56 to 69) Pineapple, cantaloupe melon and overripe bananas): watermelon

Dried apricots (medium gi (56 to 69) Sweet potato, pumpkin and parsnip): potatoes, whether baked, boiled, fried or mashed

Carrots, tomatoes, spinach, broccoli and mushrooms (medium gi (56 to 69) New potatoes and broad beans): white bread and some wholemeal breads

Beans, peas and lentils (medium gi (56 to 69) Basmati rice and couscous): bagels and doughnuts

Steel-cut oats and rye bread (medium gi (56 to 69) Chapatti): some sugary breakfast cereals

Yam and plantain (medium gi (56 to 69) Plain popcorn): sweets and sugary drinks

Unsweetened milk and yoghurt (medium gi (56 to 69) ):

Diabetes UK points out that most fruit and vegetables are low or medium GI. They also bring fibre and vitamins such as vitamin C, so there’s no need to avoid them.

The BDA’s own list adds more low GI options, including jumbo oats, unsweetened muesli, barley, bulgur wheat, quinoa and pasta cooked until al dente (still firm). Sources don’t always agree on every food: the BDA counts basmati rice as low GI, while Diabetes UK puts it in the medium band.

Is low GI always healthier?

No. Diabetes UK is clear that GI on its own doesn’t tell you whether a food is healthy.

  • Chocolate is low GI mainly because of its fat content.
  • Crisps have a lower GI than potatoes cooked without fat.
  • A baked potato is high GI but still gives you useful nutrients, especially in the skin.

A diet chosen only by GI could still be high in fat and calories. Diabetes UK says that can lead to weight gain and raise your risk of heart disease. Use GI to choose between similar foods, such as one type of bread over another, rather than as the only rule.

Why portion size matters more than GI

GI tells you how fast a food raises blood sugar, not how much carbohydrate is in your portion. The BDA says portion size often has the biggest effect on blood glucose.

That’s where glycaemic load comes in. It takes into account both the GI and the amount of carbohydrate. Diabetes UK gives a good example: pasta has a lower GI than watermelon but contains more carbohydrate, so a similar amount of pasta can raise blood sugar more.

As a rough guide, the BDA suggests a fist-sized portion of starchy food for most adults, or a quarter to a third of your plate depending on how active you are. Our guide is rice bad for diabetes shows how this works with one everyday food.

What changes the GI of a food?

The same food can have a different GI depending on how you prepare it. According to Diabetes UK and the BDA:

  1. Cooking: frying, boiling and baking all change GI. Pasta cooked al dente has a lower GI than soft, overcooked pasta.
  2. Cooling and freezing: the BDA says cooling starchy foods after cooking, and freezing or toasting bread, lowers their GI.
  3. Processing: milling and puréeing can change a food’s GI. Less processed, higher-fibre foods generally have a lower GI.
  4. Ripeness: riper fruit raises blood sugar faster. The BDA mentions yellow or brown bananas, mango and pineapple.
  5. Fibre, fat and protein: these slow digestion. Eating carbs with protein, healthy fats and vegetables lowers the overall effect of a meal.

Diabetes UK also notes that wholegrain isn’t the same as wholemeal. Wholemeal just means the grain has been ground, which is why some wholemeal breads are still high GI.

How does GI help with diabetes?

Diabetes UK says choosing low GI foods can help people with type 2 diabetes manage their long-term blood sugar (HbA1c). Swapping high GI foods for lower GI ones can also help manage blood sugar in gestational diabetes.

For type 1 diabetes, the evidence is weaker. Diabetes UK says low GI foods can still help keep blood sugar levels steady after eating.

If you take medication for diabetes, the BDA advises speaking to your healthcare professional before changing your diet. Talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian, and ask your GP about a referral to a dietitian for advice that fits you.

Easy low GI swaps to try

The BDA’s tips make GI easy to use day to day:

  • swap white bread for wholegrain, seeded, rye or oat bread
  • choose jumbo or steel-cut oats instead of instant oats
  • add beans, lentils or chickpeas to stews, soups and salads
  • keep the skins on potatoes, fruit and vegetables
  • pick less ripe fruit, and keep fruit juice to no more than 150ml a day
  • swap sugary drinks for water or herbal tea
  • have fruit and nuts, or veg sticks with hummus, instead of biscuits and crisps

For more ideas between meals, see our best snacks for type 2 diabetes.

Checking meals without a label

GI is harder to judge when you’re eating out or someone else has cooked. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the sugar, salt and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap, which can help you spot the carb-heavy parts of the plate.

item.title: DASH Diet UK: What to Eat for High Blood Pressure
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The DASH diet is an eating plan built to help lower blood pressure: more fruit, veg, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, less salt. Here's a simple UK guide. The DASH diet is an eating plan designed to help lower high blood pressure. It’s built around fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, and keeps salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol low.
item.content:encoded:
The DASH diet is an eating plan designed to help lower high blood pressure. It’s built around fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy, and keeps salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol low. You don’t need special foods, just the right balance of everyday ones.

What is the DASH diet?

DASH stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that it was designed by researchers at the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute in the 1990s.

The idea is simple: eat less salt (sodium) and more fibre, potassium and calcium. According to the BHF, that combination can help lower blood pressure.

There are no banned foods and no set meals. What matters is getting the balance of food groups right across the day.

Does the DASH diet lower blood pressure?

The BHF says many studies show the DASH diet can help bring blood pressure down to a healthy level. A 2019 review it cites, covering 7 meta-analyses, linked the diet to a 5.2mmHg drop in systolic pressure (the top number) and a 2.6mmHg drop in diastolic pressure (the bottom number).

The same review linked it to a 20 per cent lower risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack, stroke and coronary heart disease. Research also suggests it may help with cholesterol, blood sugar and weight.

For context, the BHF says high blood pressure is diagnosed at over 140/90mmHg in a clinic, or over 135/85mmHg for home readings. The NHS notes that high blood pressure doesn’t usually cause any symptoms, so the only way to know is to get it checked.

What can you eat on the DASH diet?

Here are the BHF’s daily servings for someone eating around 2,000 calories a day. If you need more or fewer calories, the number of servings changes.

Food group How much One serving is about
Vegetables 4 to 5 a day 2 handfuls of raw leafy veg, or 1 handful of other veg
Fruit 4 to 5 a day 1 medium fruit, or 3 tbsp unsweetened dried fruit
Wholegrains 7 to 8 a day 1 slice of wholemeal bread, or 1 handful of cooked wholegrain pasta or rice
Lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs Up to 6 a day 30g cooked meat or fish, or 1 egg
Low-fat or fat-free dairy 2 to 3 a day 235ml low-fat milk or yoghurt, or 43g low-fat cheese
Nuts, seeds and beans 4 to 5 a week 43g mixed nuts, 2 tbsp seeds, or 85g cooked beans
Fats and oils 2 to 3 a day 1 tsp vegetable oil or soft margarine
Added sugar and sweets Under 5 a week 1 tbsp sugar or jam
Alcohol Under 1 drink a day, or 14 units a week A single shot of spirit is 1 unit

Vegetables (how much 4 to 5 a day): 2 handfuls of raw leafy veg, or 1 handful of other veg

Fruit (how much 4 to 5 a day): 1 medium fruit, or 3 tbsp unsweetened dried fruit

Wholegrains (how much 7 to 8 a day): 1 slice of wholemeal bread, or 1 handful of cooked wholegrain pasta or rice

Lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs (how much Up to 6 a day): 30g cooked meat or fish, or 1 egg

Low-fat or fat-free dairy (how much 2 to 3 a day): 235ml low-fat milk or yoghurt, or 43g low-fat cheese

Nuts, seeds and beans (how much 4 to 5 a week): 43g mixed nuts, 2 tbsp seeds, or 85g cooked beans

Fats and oils (how much 2 to 3 a day): 1 tsp vegetable oil or soft margarine

Added sugar and sweets (how much Under 5 a week): 1 tbsp sugar or jam

Alcohol (how much Under 1 drink a day, or 14 units a week): a single shot of spirit is 1 unit

That might look like a lot of servings, but the portions are small. A handful of cooked wholegrain rice and a slice of wholemeal toast already make two wholegrain servings.

How much salt is allowed?

The BHF describes two versions of the DASH diet:

  1. Standard: no more than 2,300mg of sodium a day, about 6g or one teaspoon of salt.
  2. Lower sodium: no more than 1,500mg of sodium a day, about 4g or three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt. The BHF says this may lower blood pressure further.

Checking labels makes it easier to stay under the limit. Our guide on how much salt a day shows where it hides and how to spot high-salt foods.

Why does potassium matter?

Blood Pressure UK explains that salt makes your body hold on to water, which upsets the balance of sodium and potassium your kidneys need. Eating more potassium-rich foods helps restore that balance and lets the kidneys help lower your blood pressure.

Good sources it lists include bananas, apricots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, spinach, cabbage, sprouts, fish, yoghurt, nuts and mushrooms. That’s one reason DASH leans so heavily on fruit and veg.

A word of care, though. Blood Pressure UK says that if you have kidney disease or take certain blood pressure medicines, a large increase in potassium could be harmful. It advises avoiding potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes, and checking with your doctor first. The British Dietetic Association adds that if you have kidney disease, speak to your dietitian before changing your diet.

DASH or Mediterranean diet: which is better?

The two have a lot in common. Both are high in fish, vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, nuts and seeds, and low in salt, added sugar, saturated fat and red meat.

The BHF points out a few differences:

  • DASH includes several daily servings of low-fat dairy, because calcium is known to help lower blood pressure
  • the Mediterranean diet recommends more oily fish, a source of omega-3 fats
  • DASH is more structured, with set servings, while the Mediterranean diet is more flexible

The BHF says either can support heart health, so pick the one you can stick with.

Simple ways to start eating the DASH way

You don’t have to change everything at once. A few easy steps:

  • add a portion of fruit or veg to each meal
  • swap white bread, rice and pasta for wholegrain versions
  • switch to semi-skimmed or skimmed milk and plain low-fat yoghurt
  • have beans, lentils or unsalted nuts a few times a week
  • cook from scratch more often, and taste before adding salt
  • keep alcohol within 14 units a week, in line with NHS advice

The NHS also recommends at least 150 minutes of exercise a week alongside a healthy diet. If your blood pressure stays high after lifestyle changes, your GP may suggest medicine. Never stop or change blood pressure tablets yourself; talk to your GP or practice nurse.

Checking meals when there’s no label

Supermarket food has a label, and our guide to reading food labels explains the traffic lights. Meals out and home-cooked dishes don’t. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the salt, sugar and fat in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap that fits a DASH-style plate.

item.title: Is Rice Bad for Diabetes? Portions, Better Choices and Tips
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Rice isn't off limits with diabetes. Portion size matters most, and brown or wholegrain rice is a better pick. See UK portion guides and easy swaps. Is rice bad for diabetes? No, rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. What matters most is how much you eat, because the total amount of carbohydrate has the biggest effect on your blood sugar, and choosing brown or wholegrain rice over white where you can.
item.content:encoded:
Is rice bad for diabetes? No, rice can still be part of a healthy diet when you have diabetes. What matters most is how much you eat, because the total amount of carbohydrate has the biggest effect on your blood sugar, and choosing brown or wholegrain rice over white where you can.

Why does rice raise blood sugar?

Rice is a starchy food, and starchy foods are mostly carbohydrate. Your body breaks carbohydrate down into glucose for energy, which is why your blood sugar goes up after a rice-based meal.

Diabetes UK explains that the total amount of carbohydrate you eat has the biggest effect on your glucose levels after eating. Eating more carbohydrate than usual can push blood sugar too high.

The type of rice matters too. Diabetes UK says cooked white rice is absorbed almost as quickly as glucose from a sugary drink, which gives it a high glycaemic index (GI).

What is the glycaemic index, and where does rice fit?

GI ranks foods and drinks that contain carbohydrate from 0 to 100, based on how quickly they raise blood sugar. Diabetes UK uses these bands:

GI band Score How fast it raises blood sugar
Low 55 or below Slowly
Medium 56 to 69 At a moderate rate
High 70 or more Quickly

Low (score 55 or below): slowly

Medium (score 56 to 69): at a moderate rate

High (score 70 or more): quickly

Diabetes UK lists basmati rice as a medium GI food. It also points out that GI doesn’t account for portion size, and that the amount of carbs you eat has a bigger effect on blood sugar than GI alone.

GI also changes with cooking, processing and what you eat alongside a food. Fat, protein and fibre can all lower the GI of a meal, so rice eaten with vegetables, beans or chicken behaves differently from a plate of rice on its own.

Which rice is best for diabetes?

Diabetes UK suggests choosing brown rice instead of white, and looking out for brown basmati and quick-cook brown rice. Brown rice is a whole grain, so it keeps more of the bran and germ, where most of the nutrients are. When grains are refined, most of that is removed.

According to Diabetes UK, wholegrain foods are usually better for managing blood glucose levels, and choosing high-fibre wholegrains over refined carbs is also better for heart health. The NHS adds that brown and wholegrain rice provide fibre and B vitamins, which help release energy from food.

A quick guide to common choices:

  1. Brown basmati or quick-cook brown rice: a whole grain with more fibre, and the swap Diabetes UK recommends.
  2. White basmati: medium GI, a better pick than standard white rice if you prefer a white grain.
  3. Standard white rice: high GI, so keep portions modest and pair it with vegetables and protein.

Brown rice still contains carbohydrate and still raises blood sugar, so Diabetes UK says it’s worth keeping an eye on portion sizes whichever rice you choose.

How much rice is a portion?

Diabetes UK’s portion guide says a portion of cooked rice is about the amount that would fit in two hands cupped together, around 180g. That’s the same as its guide for boiled pasta and cooked noodles.

Some tips from Diabetes UK for getting portions right:

  • Rice can be tricky to judge at first, so weigh it, then use the same container each time
  • Don’t assume the portion on the packet suits you
  • Try smaller plates and bowls, which make portions look bigger
  • Fill part of your plate with vegetables, which are low in calories and high in fibre
  • Freeze leftover rice dishes in single portions

These portions are a guide for an average healthy adult. A dietitian can tell you the right amount for you.

What can I eat instead of rice?

You don’t have to give rice up, but variety helps. Diabetes UK suggests trying wholewheat couscous, quinoa or bulgur wheat in place of white rice. Adding pulses such as beans and lentils to a meal is another way to bring in fibre.

Fibre is worth the effort. Diabetes UK says it helps keep the digestive system healthy and helps manage blood glucose and cholesterol, and adults should aim for 30g of fibre a day.

If you’re watching carbs, Diabetes UK also says not everyone with diabetes needs to restrict their carb intake. If you take medication that can cause hypos and want to cut down, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian first so they can review it with you.

How should I store and reheat leftover rice?

Leftover rice needs a bit of care. The NHS explains that spores of some food poisoning bugs can survive cooking, and if cooked rice is left at room temperature they can produce toxins that cause vomiting and diarrhoea.

The NHS advice is to:

  • serve rice as soon as it’s cooked, or cool it within 1 hour and keep it in the fridge
  • eat refrigerated rice within 24 hours
  • throw away rice left out at room temperature overnight
  • reheat it only once, until it’s steaming hot all the way through

Checking a rice dish without a label

Packets of rice come with nutrition labels, and our guide on how to read food labels with diabetes explains them. A takeaway curry or a plate of jollof at a family gathering doesn’t. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs in a meal from a photo and suggest a swap, such as a smaller portion of rice with more vegetables. If you’re looking for lighter options between meals, see our best snacks for type 2 diabetes.

item.title: 14 Major Food Allergens UK: What They Are and Where They Hide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The 14 major food allergens in the UK, from celery to sulphites, where they hide in everyday food, and how to spot them on labels and menus. The 14 major food allergens in the UK are celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, and tree nuts.
item.content:encoded:
The 14 major food allergens in the UK are celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide and sulphites, and tree nuts. UK food law says businesses must tell you when any of them are in the food they sell, whether it’s in a supermarket pack, a bakery counter or a takeaway.

What are the 14 allergens, and where do they hide?

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) describes these 14 as the most potent and common allergens. Some are obvious. Others turn up in places you might not expect.

Allergen What it includes, and what to know
Celery Allergy UK says it’s often hidden in many foods
Cereals containing gluten Wheat, rye, barley and oats
Crustaceans Shellfish such as prawns, crab and lobster
Eggs One of the most common allergies in babies and young children
Fish Part of the wider “seafood” group, along with shellfish
Lupin Less familiar, so check ingredients lists for it
Milk Cow’s milk allergy is one of the most common in UK babies and young children
Molluscs Shellfish such as mussels and oysters
Mustard Allergy UK says it can be hidden, so you may not see, taste or smell it
Peanuts A legume that grows underground, not a tree nut
Sesame Sesame seeds, sesame oil and tahini
Soya Soya flour is common in bread, cakes, ready meals, burgers, sausages and baby foods
Sulphur dioxide and sulphites Preservatives that keep colour, flavour and shelf life, listed above 10 parts per million
Tree nuts Almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios and macadamias

Celery: Allergy UK says it’s often hidden in many foods

Cereals containing gluten: Wheat, rye, barley and oats

Crustaceans: Shellfish such as prawns, crab and lobster

Eggs: One of the most common allergies in babies and young children

Fish: Part of the wider “seafood” group, along with shellfish

Lupin: Less familiar, so check ingredients lists for it

Milk: Cow’s milk allergy is one of the most common in UK babies and young children

Molluscs: Shellfish such as mussels and oysters

Mustard: Allergy UK says it can be hidden, so you may not see, taste or smell it

Peanuts: A legume that grows underground, not a tree nut

Sesame: Sesame seeds, sesame oil and tahini

Soya: Soya flour is common in bread, cakes, ready meals, burgers, sausages and baby foods

Sulphur dioxide and sulphites: Preservatives that keep colour, flavour and shelf life, listed above 10 parts per million

Tree nuts: Almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, pecans, pistachios and macadamias

Soya is a good example of how easy it is to miss an allergen. Allergy UK says as many as 60% of manufactured foods contain soya.

Are peanuts and tree nuts the same allergen?

No. Allergy UK points out that peanuts grow underground and belong to the legume family, so they’re listed separately from tree nuts. If you’re not sure which nuts you need to avoid, ask your GP or allergy team.

Which allergies do children grow out of?

Allergy UK says egg and cow’s milk allergies are among the most common in babies and young children. Most children grow out of egg allergy by the time they start school. A small number of people don’t outgrow milk allergy, and Allergy UK says adults who still have it are more likely to have severe reactions.

Tree nut allergies are different. Allergy UK says they tend to last, and people rarely grow out of them, especially after the age of five. If you think your child’s allergy has changed, talk to your GP or allergy team.

How are allergens shown on UK food labels?

On prepacked food, the FSA says any of the 14 allergens must be emphasised in the ingredients list, for example in bold, italics or a different colour. That makes the ingredients list the place to look, not the front of the pack. Our guide on how to read food labels covers the rest of the label.

Since 1 October 2021, food that is prepacked for direct sale (PPDS) must also carry a full ingredients list with the allergens emphasised. The FSA says the label doesn’t replace talking to staff about your allergy.

What does “may contain” mean?

“May contain” or “not suitable for people with a nut allergy” are precautionary labels. They warn that an allergen could be in the food by accident, through cross-contamination during making or packing.

The FSA says there is no specific legal requirement to use these labels, so a food without one isn’t guaranteed to be free of an allergen. If you have a diagnosed allergy, ask your GP or allergy team how to treat “may contain” warnings.

What about loose food, restaurants and takeaways?

You still have the right to know what’s in your food when there’s no label:

  1. Loose food (bakeries, butchers, delis): the business must give you allergen information. It can be written or spoken, but if it’s spoken, staff must tell you where to find it in writing.
  2. Restaurants and cafés: allergen information must be on the menu, or there must be a note telling you how to get it.
  3. Takeaways and delivery: allergen information must be available before you buy and again when the food arrives.

Businesses must give you the information, but they don’t have to make you a different meal. If a business doesn’t provide allergen information, you can report it to the FSA through its “report a food problem” service, which passes it to the local council.

The 14 aren’t the only foods people react to. If your allergen isn’t on the list, the FSA advises checking the label or asking staff.

What are the signs of an allergic reaction?

The NHS lists common symptoms of a food allergy, which can affect several parts of the body at once:

  • itchy skin or a raised rash
  • swelling of the lips, face and eyes
  • sneezing or an itchy, runny or blocked nose
  • coughing, wheezing or a hoarse voice
  • feeling or being sick, tummy pain or diarrhoea
  • feeling dizzy or lightheaded

Symptoms can start straight after eating, or days later. If you think you or your child has a food allergy, see a GP.

When is it an emergency?

Call 999 straight away if lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, breathing becomes fast or difficult, the throat feels tight, skin or lips turn blue, grey or pale, or someone becomes confused, drowsy or faints. These can be signs of anaphylaxis.

If you have an adrenaline auto-injector, the NHS says to use it straight away and then call 999, even if the person seems to be getting better. Don’t drive yourself to A&E.

Checking food when there’s no label

Labels and allergen menus do the heavy lifting, but home cooking, buffets and food from friends don’t come with an ingredients list. An app like Dietary Insight can help you think it through: snap a photo of a meal and it flags ingredients that may contain common allergens on your profile. It can’t see everything in a dish, so always read the full label and ask the person who made the food.

The quick allergen checklist

  1. Learn the 14 allergens, especially the hidden ones like celery, mustard and soya.
  2. Read the ingredients list every time, even on foods you buy often.
  3. Ask staff for allergen information when food is loose, made to order or delivered.
  4. Treat “may contain” warnings the way your GP or allergy team advises.
  5. Carry your adrenaline auto-injector if you’ve been prescribed one.

item.title: Best Snacks for Type 2 Diabetes: Easy UK Ideas and Swaps
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are fruit, veg, plain yoghurt and unsalted nuts. See calorie and carb counts plus simple swaps for crisps and sweets. The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are simple, everyday foods: fresh fruit, vegetable sticks, plain yoghurt, unsalted nuts and seeds, and wholegrain crackers or oatcakes.
item.content:encoded:
The best snacks for type 2 diabetes are simple, everyday foods: fresh fruit, vegetable sticks, plain yoghurt, unsalted nuts and seeds, and wholegrain crackers or oatcakes. Diabetes UK says snacks can be part of a healthy, balanced diet, as long as you keep an eye on portions and how often you snack.

Do people with type 2 diabetes need to snack?

Not always. An NHS diabetes leaflet from Frimley Health advises that it’s best to avoid extra snacks, especially if you’re trying to lose weight. Eating more wholegrains, fruit, vegetables, beans and pulses at main meals can help you feel fuller for longer.

If you take insulin or certain medications that can cause hypos, you may need a snack between meals. Diabetes UK says this should contain some starchy carbohydrate. If you find you need frequent snacks to avoid low blood sugar, talk to your GP, diabetes nurse or dietitian.

What makes a good diabetes snack?

The Frimley Health leaflet suggests snacks with about 10 to 15g of carbohydrate and a low to medium glycaemic index (GI). Diabetes UK adds a few pointers:

  • choose snacks that are lower in saturated fat, sugar and salt
  • keep healthier snacks at home and take some out with you
  • check whether you’re really thirsty, not hungry; water or unsweetened tea or coffee may be all you need
  • skip foods labelled “diabetic”, which have no proven special benefit

Snack amounts vary by brand and pack size, so check the label on anything pre-packed. Our guide on how to read food labels with diabetes explains the traffic lights.

Which snacks are under 100 calories?

These figures come from Diabetes UK. They’re handy if you’re watching your weight as well as your blood sugar.

Snack Calories
1 kiwi fruit 25
80g blueberries 32
1 small apple (about 85g) 37
2 satsumas 44
1 light cheese triangle and 4 cherry tomatoes 43
10 almonds 61
1 crispbread, 25g cottage cheese and 4 cherry tomatoes 75
50g roasted chickpeas 79
100g cherries with 50g natural yoghurt 87.5
50g baked plantain chips 100

1 kiwi fruit: 25 calories

80g blueberries: 32 calories

1 small apple (about 85g): 37 calories

2 satsumas: 44 calories

1 light cheese triangle and 4 cherry tomatoes: 43 calories

10 almonds: 61 calories

1 crispbread, 25g cottage cheese and 4 cherry tomatoes: 75 calories

50g roasted chickpeas: 79 calories

100g cherries with 50g natural yoghurt: 87.5 calories

50g baked plantain chips: 100 calories

A little more filling, at under 150 calories: 125g natural yoghurt with 80g raspberries (119), or a 25g slice of Edam with a small apple (122).

Which snacks are lowest in carbs?

Diabetes UK lists these snacks with under 10g of carbohydrate:

  1. 1 chopped boiled egg: 0g carbs, 79 calories
  2. Half an avocado (70g): 1g carbs, 133 calories
  3. 115g pot of sugar-free jelly: 1.2g carbs, 8 calories
  4. 30g almonds: 2g carbs, 184 calories
  5. 30g houmous with 80g sliced peppers: 5g carbs, 104 calories
  6. 1 kiwi fruit: 5g carbs, 25 calories
  7. Homemade vegetable crisps: 8.4g carbs, 48 calories

Low carb doesn’t always mean low calorie. Nuts give you fibre and healthy fats, but Diabetes UK suggests watching portions if you’re managing your weight.

What can I swap for crisps, chocolate and sweets?

You don’t have to give up the snacks you love. Diabetes UK suggests these swaps:

Instead of Try
Crisps Plain popcorn, with a pinch of cinnamon if you like
Bombay mix A small handful of unsalted pumpkin or sunflower seeds
White pitta and dips Wholemeal pitta, or carrot and celery sticks with homemade hummus
Milk chocolate Two or three squares of dark chocolate
Ice cream Frozen banana, or frozen unsweetened yoghurt with berries
Chocolate biscuits Plain biscuits such as rich tea or plain digestives
Sweets Frozen grapes or frozen blueberries
Salted nuts Unsalted nuts
Sugary fizzy drinks Water flavoured with mint or fresh fruit

Instead of crisps, try plain popcorn, with a pinch of cinnamon if you like

Instead of bombay mix, try a small handful of unsalted pumpkin or sunflower seeds

Instead of white pitta and dips, try wholemeal pitta, or carrot and celery sticks with homemade hummus

Instead of milk chocolate, try two or three squares of dark chocolate

Instead of ice cream, try frozen banana, or frozen unsweetened yoghurt with berries

Instead of chocolate biscuits, try plain biscuits such as rich tea or plain digestives

Instead of sweets, try frozen grapes or frozen blueberries

Instead of salted nuts, try unsalted nuts

Instead of sugary fizzy drinks, try water flavoured with mint or fresh fruit

If you enjoy nut butter, check the label. Diabetes UK notes that some contain added sugar, salt or palm oil.

What about plantain chips, patties and other world snacks?

Diabetes UK looked at popular snacks from South Asian, African and Caribbean shops. Some pack a lot of carbs into one bag. For example, a 42.5g bag of sweet plantain chips has 27.7g of carbs and 204 calories, and a 140g jerk chicken patty has 39.3g of carbs and 345.5 calories.

Diabetes UK says the plantain chips and patty are high in saturated fat and carbs, so keep portions small. As an occasional treat, it says snacks like these can be part of a healthy diet. It suggests measuring out a portion before you reseal the packet and keeping the rest out of sight. For something you can have more often, try spicy roasted chickpeas, baked plantain chips or homemade veg crisps.

How do I stop snacking when I’m not hungry?

Boredom, emotions, nerves and anxiety can all send us to the snack cupboard. Diabetes UK suggests pausing to ask why you’re reaching for food, then trying a distraction such as calling a friend, reading or going for a walk. And if you do snack, don’t beat yourself up about it.

Late-night snacking is worth watching too. You use less energy while you sleep, so Diabetes UK says late-night snacks can lead to weight gain and affect how you manage your diabetes.

Checking snacks without a label

Packets make portions easy to compare, but a plate of leftovers or a bakery treat rarely comes with numbers. The Dietary Insight app can estimate the carbs and calories in a snack from a photo and suggest a swap, so you can see how it fits into your day. For more ideas earlier in the day, see our diabetes-friendly breakfast ideas.

item.title: 12 Diabetes-Friendly Breakfast Ideas (UK Guide)
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Simple breakfasts for type 2 diabetes built on fibre, protein and wholegrains, plus the cereal and juice traps to avoid. Quick UK ideas inside. A good breakfast for type 2 diabetes combines slow-release carbs, fibre and some protein . That mix tends to raise blood sugar more gently and keeps you full until lunch.
item.content:encoded:
A good breakfast for type 2 diabetes combines slow-release carbs, fibre and some protein. That mix tends to raise blood sugar more gently and keeps you full until lunch. There’s no special “diabetes diet”, so these are ordinary foods you can buy in any UK supermarket.

What makes a breakfast diabetes-friendly

  • Low-GI starchy foods: oats, wholegrain or multigrain bread, and wholegrain cereal instead of white bread or sugary cereal.
  • Fibre: adults should aim for 30g a day, and breakfast is an easy place to start.
  • Protein: eggs, plain yoghurt, milk, nuts or seeds help you stay full.
  • Little or no free sugar: watch the honey, syrup, jam, juice and flavoured yoghurts.

12 breakfast ideas

Quick (under 5 minutes)

  1. Porridge with berries. Make it with milk or water and add a handful of berries and a pinch of cinnamon instead of sugar.
  2. Plain Greek yoghurt with fruit and seeds. Choose unsweetened yoghurt and add berries, sliced apple or a spoon of seeds.
  3. Wholegrain toast with peanut butter. Use a thin spread of a no-added-sugar peanut butter.
  4. Wholegrain cereal with milk. Pick a cereal with green or amber for sugar, and check the per 100g figure.
  5. Melon or grapefruit with unsweetened yoghurt. A light option Diabetes UK suggests.
  6. Overnight oats. Oats soaked in milk overnight, topped with berries in the morning.

When you have more time

  1. Scrambled or poached eggs on wholegrain toast.
  2. Vegetable omelette. Peppers, spinach, mushrooms and onions.
  3. Beans on wholegrain toast. Choose reduced-sugar and reduced-salt baked beans.
  4. Smoked salmon with egg. Keep it as a treat, because smoked fish is salty.
  5. Shakshuka. Eggs baked in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce.
  6. Wholegrain pancakes. Top with berries and yoghurt instead of syrup.

Breakfast traps to watch

Instead of Try
Sugary or chocolate cereal Porridge or a plain wholegrain cereal
Fruit juice or a smoothie A piece of whole fruit and a glass of water
White toast with jam Wholegrain toast with eggs or peanut butter
Flavoured fruit yoghurt Plain yoghurt with fresh berries
Pastries and croissants Overnight oats or a vegetable omelette

Instead of sugary or chocolate cereal, try porridge or a plain wholegrain cereal

Instead of fruit juice or a smoothie, try a piece of whole fruit and a glass of water

Instead of white toast with jam, try wholegrain toast with eggs or peanut butter

Instead of flavoured fruit yoghurt, try plain yoghurt with fresh berries

Instead of pastries and croissants, try overnight oats or a vegetable omelette

Juice and smoothies count as free sugars, and they have less fibre than whole fruit. A glass of juice can raise blood sugar quickly, even with “no added sugar” on the label.

Portions still matter

A big bowl of a healthy cereal is still a lot of carbohydrate. Use a measured portion for a week to learn what one looks like. If you use insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar, talk to your diabetes team before changing your breakfast routine.

Check your breakfast in seconds

Not sure about a café breakfast or a new cereal? Snap a photo with Dietary Insight to see the sugar, fibre and protein, plus a healthier swap if there’s a better option.

item.title: How Much Salt a Day? A UK Guide for High Blood Pressure
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Adults should have no more than 6g of salt a day. Here's where it hides, how to read salt on labels and easy swaps to cut back. Adults in the UK should have no more than 6g of salt a day , about one level teaspoon. Eating too much salt can raise blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.
item.content:encoded:
Adults in the UK should have no more than 6g of salt a day, about one level teaspoon. Eating too much salt can raise blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Most of it isn’t from the salt shaker.

Where your salt really comes from

The NHS says about three quarters of the salt we eat is already in food when we buy it. The biggest sources are everyday foods:

  • bread and breakfast cereals
  • ham, bacon, sausages and other processed meat
  • ready meals, takeaways and restaurant food
  • sauces such as soy sauce, gravy granules, ketchup and brown sauce
  • cheese, olives, pickles and smoked or cured fish

None of these tastes especially salty, which is why salt is easy to overdo.

Daily salt limits by age

Age Maximum salt a day
Adults and children 11+ 6g
7 to 10 years 5g
4 to 6 years 3g
1 to 3 years 2g
Under 1 year Less than 1g

Adults and children 11+: 6g

7 to 10 years: 5g

4 to 6 years: 3g

1 to 3 years: 2g

Under 1 year: Less than 1g

Salt or sodium? Do the conversion

Some labels list sodium instead of salt. Multiply sodium by 2.5 to get the salt figure. So 0.6g of sodium is 1.5g of salt, which is already a quarter of an adult’s daily limit.

Reading salt on a food label

Per 100g of food:

  • Low (green): 0.3g of salt or less
  • High (red): more than 1.5g of salt

Compare similar products per 100g. Two loaves or two jars of pasta sauce can differ a lot.

8 easy swaps to cut back

  1. Cook from scratch more often, so you control the salt.
  2. Flavour food with herbs, spices, garlic, chilli, lemon or black pepper.
  3. Taste before you add salt at the table, or leave the shaker in the cupboard.
  4. Choose reduced-salt stock cubes and gravy, and use less.
  5. Swap processed meat sandwiches for chicken, egg or bean fillings.
  6. Rinse tinned beans and vegetables canned in brine.
  7. Ask for sauces on the side when you eat out.
  8. Snack on unsalted nuts, fruit or veg sticks instead of crisps.

Your taste buds adjust within a few weeks, and food that once tasted bland starts to taste normal.

A word on salty medicines

Some dissolvable tablets, such as certain painkillers and vitamins, contain a surprising amount of salt. Don’t stop any medicine on your own. Ask your GP or pharmacist whether there’s a lower-salt version.

Checking meals without a label

Takeaways and restaurant food are some of the saltiest meals, and they rarely show a figure. An app like Dietary Insight can estimate the salt in a meal from a photo, so you can see when one dish uses up most of your day’s allowance.

item.title: How to Read UK Food Labels When You Have Diabetes
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: A simple guide to UK traffic-light labels, hidden sugar names and per-100g figures, so you can choose better food in the supermarket in seconds. Most UK food packs carry a traffic-light label on the front. Learn three numbers and you can judge sugar, fat and salt in a few seconds, without a calculator.
item.content:encoded:
Most UK food packs carry a traffic-light label on the front. Learn three numbers and you can judge sugar, fat and salt in a few seconds, without a calculator.

The traffic-light label in 10 seconds

Green means low, amber means medium and red means high. A pack that is mostly green and amber is a good everyday choice. Any red means that food is best eaten less often or in smaller amounts.

These are the NHS thresholds per 100g of food:

Per 100g Low (green) High (red)
Total fat 3g or less More than 17.5g
Saturated fat 1.5g or less More than 5g
Sugars 5g or less More than 22.5g
Salt 0.3g or less More than 1.5g

Total fat (low (green) 3g or less): more than 17.5g

Saturated fat (low (green) 1.5g or less): more than 5g

Sugars (low (green) 5g or less): more than 22.5g

Salt (low (green) 0.3g or less): more than 1.5g

Anything between the two columns is amber. Drinks use different thresholds, so treat these figures as a guide for food.

Always compare per 100g, not per portion

Manufacturers choose their own portion sizes, and they are often smaller than what people really eat. When you compare two cereals or two yoghurts, use the per 100g column. It’s the only fair comparison.

Quick tip: if you’d eat twice the “portion” on the pack, double every number on the front label.

Spot hidden sugar in the ingredients

Ingredients are listed by weight, with the biggest first. Sugar often hides under other names, and a product can use several of them so none appears near the top. Look out for:

  • glucose, fructose, sucrose, dextrose, maltose
  • corn syrup and high-fructose corn syrup
  • honey, molasses, treacle, maple syrup and agave syrup
  • fruit juice concentrate and fruit purées
  • cane sugar and brown sugar

UK guidance says adults should have no more than 30g of free sugars a day, about 7 sugar cubes. Free sugars include sugar added to food and the sugar in honey, syrups and fruit juice. They don’t include the sugar naturally found in whole fruit, vegetables and milk.

Why “total sugars” can mislead

The label shows total sugars, which mixes natural and added sugar. A plain yoghurt shows some sugar from milk, which is fine. A fruit yoghurt might show double that because of added sugar. Check the ingredients list to tell them apart.

Skip foods labelled “diabetic”

Diabetes UK advises against foods sold as “diabetic”. They have no proven benefit, they often cost more, and some are still high in fat and calories. A normal, balanced choice is better.

When there is no label

Restaurant meals, takeaways and home cooking don’t come with a traffic light. That’s where most of us guess. Fill half the plate with vegetables or salad, keep starchy carbs to about a quarter, and choose grilled over fried where you can.

You can also photograph the plate with an app such as Dietary Insight. It estimates the sugar, salt and fat in the meal and flags anything that clashes with your health profile.

The 3-second checklist

  1. Look for red on the front. More red means “sometimes”, not “every day”.
  2. Compare similar products using the per 100g figures.
  3. Scan the first three ingredients for sugar under another name.

item.title: What Is Prediabetes and Can It Be Reversed? A UK Guide
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel
item.description: Prediabetes means blood sugar is above normal but below type 2 diabetes. Learn the HbA1c numbers, who is at risk and the changes that can help.
